    ]]>         ‘Too many lawyers’: the problem with Europe’s human rights NGOs https://euobserver.com/240984/too-many-lawyers-the-problem-with-europes-human-rights-ngos/ Fri, 16 Oct 2026 09:17:56 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240984 Traditionally, human rights NGOs have been staffed mainly by lawyers. This is understandable. But advocacy is becoming less effective because decision makers increasingly see supporting human rights as politically risky.]]> Human rights NGOs in Europe are not doing well. Funding cuts, legal restrictions, administrative burdens and smear campaigns are taking their toll.

    I see organisations drastically downsizing or closing altogether and staff burning out. If we are to reverse our fortunes, the traditionally legally-focused movement needs to rebalance its skill-set to include more communicators and organisers.

    Traditionally, human rights NGOs have been staffed mainly by lawyers. This is understandable. Human rights are legal standards contained in national, European and international law. If your main tools for getting human rights implemented are advocacy and litigation, then you need legal experts. But advocacy is becoming less effective because decision makers increasingly see supporting human rights as politically risky.

    And litigation as a tool is partly limited by increasing political interference with the courts in some countries, or because – again – politicians see potential political brownie points in not complying with (or see potential political costs in complying with) judgments that enforce human rights standards.

    It’s not just that NGOs’ traditional tools are losing their power. It’s that legal training does not equip us with the tools do we need to reverse our fortunes.

    Our main lever for restoring human rights and the organisations that promote them is public opinion. For as long as we live continue to live in democracies, pressure from voters can have an impact on decision makers. Which means we need communicators who can help the public realise how important human rights are to them.

    David Attenborough pointed out a few years ago that “saving our planet is now a communications challenge. We know what to do, we just need the will”.

    The same goes for human rights. 

    But legal training does not make you good at communicating with folks outside your bubble.

    Read more

    [Interview] Civil society leader to EU: ‘Stop the witch hunt on NGOs before it’s too late for democracy’

    ‘Legal-ese’ is not the right lingo

    I know from personal experience. I trod a path to human rights through a law degree, masters, doctorate and then academia. Human rights folks talk about them in a way that conveys a fraction of their value and power. If you’d asked me 15 years ago why human rights are important, I’d have said things like this: ‘they protect us from abuse by the government’, or ‘they’re minimum standards of protection the state can’t breach’, or ‘they exist to protect the vulnerable’.

    These things are true. They’re also not very persuasive to people outside our base of support. Because the kinds of human rights breaches the movement foregrounds tend to affect ‘other people’. And lawyers are used to thinking about rights in the context of legal disputes.

    So human rights get reduced to a shield that protects groups or institutions that most people don’t care about, don’t understand, or who live in other countries. 

    Human rights are not just a passive defence. They are transformational. Human rights are tools. Tools we use to demand that our leaders use the powers and resources with which we’ve entrusted them to do what’s best for all of us. Tools that we use to create the lives we want to live and the communities we want to live in. This is how we need to talk about them, especially when it comes to civil and political rights.

    People outside our base cannot be made to care about media freedom, the right to protest or democracy itself just on principle or because they’re enshrined in legal standards. To care about human rights, most people need to know what these things deliver.

    Read more

    EU’s 2026 rule‑of‑law report doesn’t trigger real action, says human rights watchdog

    Folks will see that protest is important when we explain how it allows people like them to come together and make their leaders listen to their concerns, whether it’s about climate change or better pay for teachers. I’ve seen it first-hand when testing messages in focus groups. 

    Empathy, not stereotypes

    The same goes for stimulating support for the rights of people from marginalised groups. Right now, most people have trouble caring because they been fed negative stereotypes that cause them to regard some people as ‘others’ and ‘outgroups’, meaning that they will tolerate lower standards of treatment for them.

    Using legal arguments and evidencing rights violations by focusing on the harm being suffered doesn’t work because it does nothing to address the reason people don’t care. For that, we need to stimulate empathy and dissolve negative stereotypes through techniques like storytelling. Once people empathise and recognise our common humanity, they’re much more likely to support equal treatment. 

    Read more

    How NGOs die — Europe’s playbook for dismantling democracy

    When we communicate in a way that allows our audience to see how human rights deliver things they find important to them, they don’t just start to support human rights as standards. They also start to support the organisations that promote them. That means they’re more likely to listen to them, stand up for them, get involved in their work and even donate. 

    It’s not just about communicating better. We also need organisers who can help people come together to carry effective messages and make the strength of public support felt by our leaders. 

    Folks with legal training are still essential.

    If you’re going to make phones, you need engineers. But we don’t see the engineers being given the job of persuading folks to buy the phones, do we?

    Unless they’ve had proper communications training. The human rights movement’s legalistic centre of gravity needs to shift to make room for knowledge and skills that can meet the moment.

    In the short-term we could achieve this by retraining staff and joining forces with other progressive movements that know how to organise and mobilise, like environmental NGOs.

    We could also tackle the issue upstream by working with universities that produce human rights graduates to develop more holistic curricula that cover communications and organising and not only law. 

    ]]>         Listen: Are the Gilets Jaunes in France making a comeback? https://euobserver.com/243068/listen-are-the-gilets-jaunes-in-france-making-a-comeback/ Fri, 16 Oct 2026 08:35:45 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243068 Do you remember the Yellow Vests movement that shook France 2018? On TikTok, a young user has called for a national mobilisation on 17 October against the cost of living, and the video quickly went viral. So could the Yellow Vests make their big return?]]>

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below:

    Do you remember the Yellow Vests movement that shook France 2018? On TikTok, a young user has called for a national mobilisation on the seventeenth of October against the cost of living, and the video quickly went viral. So could the Yellow Vests make their big return?

    “Please, give us a date, we’re ready to protest! We young people are struggling. We just can’t make a living anymore,” that’s what Justine, a TikToker from Normandy in France has posted a few weeks ago, while wearing a fluorescent yellow vest.

    The reference to the 2018 Yellow Vests is unmistakable. The French movement, which began in protest at rising fuel prices, has been widely revived on social media in recent weeks, especially by younger users.

    Our colleague Romane Lizée from StreetPress, a fellow member of the Sphera Network alongside Europod, spoke to some of them: young people reviving a protest movement they only knew from a distance.

    Read more

    Yellow Vests leaders and ex-EU officials team up to give Europeans more say in how they are governed

    Yves, a 24-year-old TikToker with over 80,000 followers, made a video called “Survival Guide for the Yellow Vests 2026”. He gives would-be protesters practical advice, such as bringing thick ski goggles or writing a lawyer’s phone number on a piece of paper.

    So why is the movement resurfacing now? For many, the movement has come to stand for a general sense of being fed up, something they still feel today.

     “Eight years ago, France put on the yellow vest because petrol hit 1.50 euros a litre, and now we’re almost at three euros and nothing is happening!” That’s how Saïd, a 23-year-old delivery driver, sees it.

    The economic context is indeed worse than it was eight years ago. The price of fuel is now almost 2.40 euros a litre.

    Throughout September, a series of protests followed one another, called by different professions and for different reasons: climate action, firefighters, a public-sector strike, the law on sexual violence, and finally the student blockades.

    High school students have been protesting for a few weeks now, blockading their schools to demand better conditions. We talked about this in a previous Briefed episode. You can find the link in the description.

    Now, will the protest be as big and long-lasting as the one in 2018?

    Read more

    French school protests to continue, after prime minister ignores demands

    Online, a petition launched by the website 17octobregiletjaune, which calls for the protest, has gathered more than 21,000 signatures. Over a thousand actions across the country have been identified on a map by the same website: mostly protests in several cities, but also actions on roundabouts and at petrol stations.

    Youth organisations, students’ unions and education staff have already answered the call. More importantly, the CGT, one of France’s main labour unions, has backed it, as have some political figures, like Marine Tondelier, the Green candidate for the presidential election. Still, the true extent of the movement is difficult to predict.

    In other European countries, protests are also multiplying, especially among young people. In Spain, huge demonstrations for the right to housing have been taking place in several cities since mid-September. They went quite far: they pushed Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to call snap elections.

    Read more

    [Interview] Spanish socialist MEP sees no other leader than Sánchez, as housing and immigration dominate snap election

    In Brussels, on October 9th, thousands of protesters, including rail workers, teachers, and university and secondary school students, marched against the federal government’s policies, in particular its socio-economic measures. Here again, precarity is a central grievance.

    In Italy, on October 8th, students called for mobilisation, notably by camping in front of universities across the country to protest against the sharp rise in tuition fees and student rents.

    The triggers behind these protests are not all the same, and the mobilisations take different forms from country to country. But the goal is broadly the same: to call for better living conditions and to defend basic social rights. And young people are particularly mobilised.

    ]]>         Pressure mounts on EU leaders to strike a budget deal by December https://euobserver.com/243045/pressure-mounts-on-eu-leaders-to-strike-a-budget-deal-by-december/ Thu, 15 Oct 2026 22:03:22 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243045 EU Council president Antonio Costa has been tasked to deliver a new compromise before EU leaders meet again on 26 November in Brussels, with the aim to strike a deal during the summit in December - after the Irish proposal failed to gain any support.]]> EU leaders met Thursday (15 October) for their first face-to-face talks on the 2028–2034 budget, killing the latest negotiation proposal put forward by Ireland.

    Dublin, which holds the symbolic EU Council presidency, proposed cuts of up to €141bn from the long-term budget,  about eight percent less than the commission proposal. But it failed to make anybody happy, for different reasons. 

    And now, EU Council president António Costa has been tasked to deliver a new compromise before EU leaders meet again on 26 November in Brussels, with the goal of striking a deal during the summit in December. 

    An EU official said Costa deemed the deal in December as “essential,” urging EU capitals “to assume their responsibility”.

    For Denmark, for example, it is important to have more funds for defence, borders, illegal migration, and competitiveness. “It will probably be as difficult as it was last time or even more difficult,” said Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen ahead of the meeting.

    “We need unanimity in the Council. We are far from that unanimity,” also said German chancellor Friedrich Merz before meeting counterparts.

    The EU is divided into two camps. The so-called Frugals (Germany, Austria, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, and Sweden) want “several hundred billion” more to be cut, mostly from agriculture and cohesion funds, while 17 EU member states (self-named as Friends of Cohesion) criticise the savings. 

    But time is of the essence to reach a deal this year, especially for French president Emmanuel Macron. France will hold presidential elections in the spring, and if Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally party, wins, reaching an EU deal would become far more difficult.

    Le Pen has pledged that, if she comes to power, she will halve France’s contribution to the EU budget.

    And Macron reportedly said in the room with EU leaders that from January onwards, there will be no political room for reaching an agreement.

    ‘Easier to give up what you don’t yet have’

      <title>HelloFresh workers claim physical abuse and denied bathroom breaks in class-action suit</title>

      <description><p>The meal kit delivery service denies the allegations, saying it found claims to be ‘entirely without merit’</p><p>Workers at a HelloFresh facility in Newark, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/new-jersey">New Jersey</a>, have claimed in court documents that they were verbally and physically abused and denied regular bathroom breaks, with one former worker telling the Guardian he experienced incontinence issues as a result.</p><p>The newly proposed amended complaint comes in a class-action lawsuit first filed in August 2024 against the food prep service giant and staffing agencies.       <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/16/isabella-weber-anti-fascist-economics</link>
      <description><p>Exclusive: Isabella Weber prescribes a common-sense solution to poverty, inequality and fascism – making life’s essentials affordable for all</p><p>The trouble with economists, Isabella Weber believes, is they do not behave like dentists. They obsess over ideological purity and are inflexible when searching for solutions, regardless of society’s symptoms. Dentists have no such pretensions – patients have little patience for dogma when in insufferable pain.</p><p>John Maynard Keynes, Weber clarifies in the canteen of the <em>Wissenschaftskolleg zu Berlin</em> (Berlin’s Institute for Advanced Study), was the first to draw this dental comparison – and she is running with it. As she sees it, the symptoms could not be more severe. “The status quo for the majority is entirely unbearable,” while extreme inequality and corporate concentration has reached levels “simply incompatible with democracy” worldwide. This is exacerbated by a climate crisis that “generates massive windfall profits” for big business as the “ecological foundations of our lives disintegrate”. All the while the far right is making hay.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/16/isabella-weber-anti-fascist-economics">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Mines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in Indonesia</p><p>Volkswagen, Ford and Tesla are among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction.</p><p>Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot in Indonesia that houses the world’s largest nickel deposits.       <description><p>We’d like to hear about whether you feel like the US is in a recession and what you think signals such a downturn</p><p>Nearly two-thirds of Americans think the US is experiencing a recession, according to a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/voters-economy-cost-of-living-prices-poll">new Harris Poll</a> conducted for the Guardian. Still, Americans are facing <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/14/inflation-numbers-september">higher prices</a> and a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/02/september-jobs-report">stagnant job market</a>, which for many feels like a downturn.</p><p>We want to hear from Americans: do you feel like the US is experiencing a recession? What is your so-called personal “recession indicator”, or a signal in your everyday life that points to an incoming economic slump? It could be seen in your job or at your local grocery store, something you notice at your children’s school or out in your community. Tell us about it below.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/what-is-your-personal-recession-indicator">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Voters’ opposition to the state of Trump’s economy is well established – despite his desperate attempts to deflect</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/what-is-your-personal-recession-indicator">Tell us: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?</a></p></li></ul><p>It’s indisputable that the political polarization of our time has reduced (and confused) the influence of economic conditions on US elections.</p><p>In September of 2024, in the waning weeks of the Joe Biden presidency, 65% of Republicans believed the US economy was getting worse.       <link>https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oct/15/food-delivery-apps-cost-economy</link>
      <description><p>As Americans use apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats more habitually, they confront the guilt of paying extra fees for convenience</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/what-is-your-personal-recession-indicator">Tell us: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?</a></p></li></ul><p>When it comes to food, Caroline Bauldree does not like to “deprive” herself of anything. She does not like to cook either, so that means a lot of food deliveries. “If I want sushi, I’m getting sushi,” said the 24-year-old nanny, who lives in Raleigh, North Carolina. “I’m definitely lazy in that regard.”</p><p>Bauldree got into the habit of near-daily DoorDashing back in college. “I could order whatever food from whatever restaurant and it showed up at my door – that’s the dream,” she said. “But then I just feel like crap about myself because I’m like, ‘wow, I’m a lazy piece of shit.’ Nine times out of 10, I feel bad about myself.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oct/15/food-delivery-apps-cost-economy">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Is punishing the poor Trump’s last hand to play?</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms</link>
      <description><p>The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees looks like political madness – but the president appears to believe hitting poor people might work for him</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/community/live/2026/oct/14/us-economy-affordability-midterm-elections-republicans-trump">Our reporters answer your questions on whether Trump’s economy will sink Republicans in the US midterms</a></p></li></ul><p>There is a manic quality to <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/us-midterm-elections-2026">midterm elections</a> to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away.</p><p>The US president <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/28/trump-cattle-ranchers-beef-imports-backlash">offered</a> to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/23/trump-beef-imports-midterms-gop-panic-01090261">backtracking</a> under <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/25/trump-republican-backlash-beef-tariff-import">pressure</a> from the cow lobby. He <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/22/trump-diesel-export-ban">offered</a> to stop diesel exports, only to find oil companies <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/market-chatter-us-oil-executives-112235250.html">were</a> <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/chevron-ceo-diesel-export-ban-trump-supply.html">not interested</a>. He weakened fuel efficiency standards, claiming this would trim the price of a new car (and forgetting to point out it will also raise spending on gas). In early October he started mailing <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/01/economy/trump-obamacare-500-check">$500 checks</a> to nearly a million people touting his healthcare “wins”. Oh, and he promised adult Americans a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-5000-midterm-cash-dividend-response">$5,000 check</a> if Republicans maintain control of Congress. That, too, will <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-dividend-republican-midterm-convention">go nowhere</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comMon, 19 Oct 2026 23:51:57 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Ex-Labour Court chairman subject to dignity-at-work complaint from senior official, WRC told]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/19/ex-labour-court-chairman-subject-to-dignity-at-work-complaint-from-senior-official-wrc-hears/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/19/ex-labour-court-chairman-subject-to-dignity-at-work-complaint-from-senior-official-wrc-hears/Mon, 19 Oct 2026 17:56:35 +0000A former chairman of the Labour Court was the subject of a dignity-at-work complaint by an ordinary member of the court who has now claimed unfair dismissed, the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) has heard

The complainant, Peter DR Murphy, who sat as a member of the Labour Court from 2005 to 2024 as a nominee of business group Ibec, is pursuing allegations of unfair dismissal and other rights breaches against the Minister for Enterprise.

The State said Ibec did not nominate Murphy for a further term after his last warrant expired in 2024. Murphy’s legal team has said the department did not seek replacement nominees from the business group when the warrant ran out.

Murphy, a qualified solicitor, had been earning more than €140,000 a year in the role.

He alleged he was subject to workplace bullying during his appointment and he specifically identified a former chairman in a formal dignity-at-work complaint, according to legal correspondence in 2020 opened to a hearing on Monday.

Tara Coogan, a civil servant at the Department of Enterprise who was in charge of the section overseeing the Labour Court and the WRC at the end of Murphy’s last term on the court, gave evidence on the respondent’s preliminary objection to the case going ahead on Monday.

Frances Meenan, for the State, asked Coogan about a legal letter of October 5th, 2020, to former minister for enterprise Damien English from the complainants’ former solicitors.

In the letter, read out by Coogan, Murphy’s then solicitors wrote: “Our client has grave concerns about recent steps regarding the renewal of his warrant.”

The alleged change in practice was “not coincidental and is a direct response to certain recent events and issues raised by our client in respect of his working conditions and the treatment he has been forced to endure in the workplace”, the letter also said.

The letter stated Murphy had raised statutory claims concerning “bullying, victimisation and other related matters” and had “also instituted internal complaint against the chairman of the Labour Court under the Civil Service dignity at work policy”.

At that point, Meenan intervened and said: “We won’t mention any names.”

Coogan said: “I don’t know anything about this letter.”

Meenan said the State would present evidence that the complaints referenced in the letter “were subsequently withdrawn by the complainant”.

Tiernan Lowey, for the complainant, said: “We’re happy for the letter to be read out in full.”

The tribunal has heard how Murphy received one further term on the court before his final warrant lapsed in February 2024.

Meenan said it was position of the State that Murphy was not an employee and therefore had no standing to pursue the claim.

She said appointment to the Labour Court was contingent on Murphy being put forward as a nominee by Ibec, and accordingly Murphy’s 19 years at the Labour Court came to an end, Meenan said.

However, Lowey said: “We don’t believe there ever was any correspondence from the department or on behalf of the department [to Ibec] when Murphy’s last warrant expired.”

Lowey said Murphy “was never regarded as anything other than an employee of the minister”. The complainant’s position is that it had become the custom and practice to renew warrants until a member of the court resigned and only then seek three nominees.

Meenan accepted the State had “a gap” in its supporting documentation as copies of correspondence between the department and Ibec asking the employers’ group to put forward a nominee for the court every time Murphy had been reappointed were not with its legal papers.

She said the documents in question were “old paper files that are hard to get”.

Adjudicator Christina Ryan said it was “unusual” that the State was not ready with the documents in question when it was making the nomination process a “central feature” of its case.

She directed the State to produce the material and said the matter could be revisited when the case resumed on Wednesday.

Murphy’s complaints are under the Unfair Dismissals Act, the Protection of Employees (Fixed-Term Work) Act, the Redundancy Payments Act and the Minimum Notice and Terms of Employment Act.

]]><![CDATA[France unrest pushes European shares down despite tech rebound]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/19/european-shares-dip-despite-tech-rebound/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/19/european-shares-dip-despite-tech-rebound/Mon, 19 Oct 2026 17:25:20 +0000European shares dipped despite a tech rebound, as protests in France continued and weighed on sentiment.

Triggered by rising prices and worsening public services, the protests have soured investor sentiment towards a country already grappling with weak growth and rising debt.

Dublin

The Irish market started on a negative note, ending the opening session of the week in the red. The Euronext Dublin dipped 0.8 per cent to end the day at 14,069, dragged lower by weakness in banking and some construction stocks.

AIB lost 1 per cent over the day, finishing at €10.84, while Bank of Ireland was 2.46 per cent lower at €18.40. Insurer FBD was also off the pace, shedding 0.5 per cent.

Insulation specialist Kingspan declined by 1.5 per cent, and Cairn fell almost 0.6 per cent. But rival home builder Glenveagh added almost half a per cent over the session, ending the day at €2.34.

Ryanair, meanwhile, was slightly lower at €22.75, a decline of 0.1 per cent.

London

In London, the FTSE 100 Index ended down 117.21 points, 1.1 per cent, at 10,764.69.

Miners were a weak feature after mixed economic data in China and worries over the demand outlook for artificial intelligence (AI).

Anglo American shares fell 4.1 per cent, Glencore lost 3.3 per cent, while Rio Tinto dipped 1.5 per cent. Barclays declined 3.5 per cent.

The Bank of England is examining whether Barclays traders misrepresented illiquid private credit loans to understate their risk after an insider raised concerns, the Financial Times reported on Monday.

On the FTSE 250, Volex fell 12 per cent despite predicting financial 2027 underlying operating profit will be towards the upper end of current market expectations.

The Hampshire-based maker of power and data transmission products, said trading in the half-year ended September 30th was “excellent”, with year-on-year growth in every end-market.

But it cautioned headline year-on-year growth rates have started to “normalise”.

Europe

French equities suffered their worst day in nearly two weeks on Monday, weighing on European shares after rioting erupted in cities across ​the country over the weekend.

France’s blue-chip CAC 40 index fell 1.1 per cent, while the pan-European STOXX 600 index slipped 0.9 per cent to 639.1 points.

French lenders BNP Paribas, Société Générale and Credit Agricole fell between 2.5 per cent ⁠and 3.4 per cent. Retailer Carrefour declined 2.2 per cent and shopping mall ​operator Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield dropped 2 per cent.

Political uncertainty ​also came to the fore in Spain, where the equities benchmark fell 1.5 per cent. A snap election scheduled for next month ‌has left investors wary.

Cyclical sectors led declines across Europe, with banks the biggest laggards following a 2.2 per cent decline. Defence stocks also came under pressure, falling 1.5 per cent.

The technology index was the only big index in positive territory, rising 0.7 per cent. Last week, European shares held up better than US peers during a sell-off in AI-linked stocks over concerns about rising debt to fund infrastructure spending.

New York

Meanwhile, Tan’s reference to “very extreme expectations” may have been aimed at investors, but extraordinary expectations of AI are apparently evident elsewhere in the industry. Then there is Anthropic, which is moving to prohibit sustained cruelty towards its Claude chatbot, despite the absence of evidence that the software experiences suffering.

Clueless investors with extreme expectations are one thing, but researchers smoking in anticipation of a cure for cancer and developers worrying about a chatbot’s feelings suggest the AI boom is acquiring some distinctly unusual characteristics.

]]>Bloomberg<![CDATA[Looming elections place burden on Ireland to find EU budget compromise]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/19/looming-elections-place-burden-on-ireland-to-find-eu-budget-compromise/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/19/looming-elections-place-burden-on-ireland-to-find-eu-budget-compromise/Mon, 19 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000Ireland’s EU presidency has the job of brokering a deal on the EU’s budget for the years from 2028-2034. Getting a majority will be difficult between those member states who want a bigger, and others a smaller, budget. There is, however, an urgency to strike a deal before possible changes in government after forthcoming elections make reaching agreement even more challenging.

Marine le Pen, for example, believes in dramatically reducing the EU’s role and returning powers to national governments. If she wins the French presidential election next May, she could seek to upend EU funding.

To judge by the rows over recent decades about the EU’s budget, you might believe it is a major drain on member states’ national resources. However, the budget amounts to only 1.1 per cent of national income, whereas national budgets across the EU average 45 per cent of national income, somewhat higher than for Ireland.

So the fight over whether the budget should amount to 1 per cent or 1.25 per cent of national income is about relatively small sums when averaged across the EU. In national budgets, such a small difference as a share of national income could get lost in rounding errors.

There are a range of public goods that are best undertaken on a pan-EU basis rather than by national governments. Examples include cross-border infrastructure, research and development, climate, security, foreign policy, industrial policy and development aid. These are areas where collective EU spending is more effective than uncoordinated national investment.

European Commission unhappy with EU budget but Taoiseach says compromise had to be made

The construction of the electricity interconnector between Ireland and France is a prime example that merits the significant EU funding involved. This project will benefit not only Ireland and France, but also the wider EU electricity system.

Interconnection across borders boosts efficiency, provides better matching of variable supply and demand, and minimises wasted power generation.

Other potentially beneficial projects to enable the free flow of electricity across the EU’s national boundaries are only likely to proceed if there is EU financial support.

Food shortages in the aftermath of the second World War were the initial driving force behind the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy. Today, however, it is more difficult to justify rationally why agriculture looms so large in the EU’s budget, or why the EU rather than national governments should fund farm supports.

Europe rearms: files reveal extent of plans for a new ‘defence union’

Ireland, of course, has benefited disproportionately from EU payments to farmers over the past half century. Like other EU members, we pay about 1 per cent of national income into the EU budget. However, despite the fact that we are one of the richest EU members, we get back around 0.7 per cent of national income, most of it going to Irish farmers. A great deal.

The modernising of Ireland’s infrastructure has also benefited greatly from EU support to poorer regions over the first decades of EU membership.

Today there are two groups of countries with very different outlooks on the EU’s budget.

The “frugals”, like Scandinavia, Germany and the Netherlands, want a smaller budget, in particular they want to cut back on funds for agriculture, and for infrastructure in poorer states. They want to reallocate funds to other headings.

The “friends of cohesion”, which include Spain, Italy and some poorer member states, want a larger budget, with continuing substantial agriculture and cohesion payments.

The first stab at a compromise by the Irish presidency involved a small cut in the original EU Commission budget proposal. For 2028-34, this proposed that real EU resources, after debt interest, would be slightly lower than today.

The Irish Times view on the EU budget: a key task for Ireland’s presidency

This draft also largely protected agriculture and cohesion funds. But this compromise got a widespread thumbs down.

In the next round of negotiations, Ireland needs to adjust its proposals to garner more support. Next time, the Bruegel think tank in Brussels suggests, we should propose a slightly larger budget that cuts back on agriculture and cohesion funds, which are unpopular with the frugals, and that reallocates some resources to other European public goods.

A few rounds of proposals may be needed to garner the necessary majority support before year end.

As the honest broker, it may thus fall to the Irish Government to propose a compromise budget that would cut some resources for agriculture, which will be unpopular at home.

However, given the risk that delayed agreement could mean an even more unpalatable outcome, as the political winds shift in France and elsewhere, it is vital from an Irish point of view that agreement is reached on the budget by the end of the year. Better a budget with somewhat reduced funds for agriculture, than no budget and no funds.

]]>LockieCurrie<![CDATA[Are many Irish homeowners undervaluing the cost of rebuilding their homes by €83,000?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/18/neglect-an-expensive-error-when-it-comes-to-insurance/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/18/neglect-an-expensive-error-when-it-comes-to-insurance/Sun, 18 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000There’s nothing like a big number to frighten consumers, especially when it comes to them being left out of pocket at a time of crisis.

Insurer Outsurance this week estimated that many homeowners could be undervaluing the cost of rebuilding or replacing their homes by about €83,000

Underinsurance can very quickly turn a drama into a financial crisis. Bad enough to have your home hit by flood, fire or other catastrophe without discovering your insurer will not cover the cost of putting things right.

People assume that if they have, say, €400,000 of insurance cover, any claim up to that value will be met. But that’s not the way it works.

If the cost of rebuilding your home is €600,000 but you only have cover for two-thirds of that (€400,000), the insurer will only cover two-thirds of every claim – even one for say €20,000 to repair flood damage – leaving homeowners thousands of euro out of pocket.

No one actually knows how pervasive the problem is.

Back in 2021, the Central Bank of Ireland sent a shot across insurers’ bows after a study by its staff discovered the level of underinsurance had surged from 6.5 per cent in 2017 to 16.5 per cent – not far short of 400,000 homes.

That figure, like the Outsurance average, emerged only from an analysis of actual claims made. We have no way of knowing how many others are underinsured. That’s not helped by the insurers themselves, Outsurance included, being remarkably coy on the subject.

In answer to a parliamentary question late last year, then minister for finance Paschal Donohoe said the figure had fallen to 10.7 per cent in 2024. Even if that claim reflects the wider market, there are still more than 230,000 homeowners at risk.

As Bank of Ireland noted in 2026, the trend over recent years to invest in upgrading and extending properties, including retrofits, solar panels and the like, could be making things worse.

All increase the rebuilding cost in case of disaster, but the bank found that six in 10 homeowners never update their insurance details after investing to improve their homes.

With winter looming, now would be a good time to make sure you have the cover you think you have ... before anything goes wrong.

]]>Alamy<![CDATA[Elon Musk’s trillion-dollar pay deal has a convenient escape clause]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/18/musks-trillion-dollar-pay-deal-has-a-convenient-escape-clause/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/18/musks-trillion-dollar-pay-deal-has-a-convenient-escape-clause/Sun, 18 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000A million robotaxis, a million humanoid robots, and an $8.5 trillion valuation – Elon Musk’s trillion-dollar Tesla bonus appears to demand almost superhuman performance.

There is, however, an easier (and less-publicised) way for Musk to collect the big bucks: just sell the company.

A recent study of executive pay finds that enormous share awards usually fail to deliver for shareholders and that “milestones are far less demanding than they appear”, with Musk’s 2025 Tesla package offering a striking illustration of the risks.

In Merging to the Moon: Astronomical Option Awards and Corporate Governance Failures, researchers examined 1.24 million insider stock awards between 1996 and 2022. They found that Tesla-style “mega-grants” subsequently underperformed comparable companies by 15 to 30 per cent over following years.

Tesla’s 2025 agreement offers Musk 424 million shares if the company reaches an $8.5 trillion market value and meets 12 demanding business milestones.

Considered in isolation, the package looks like a properly designed pay-for-performance deal. Under the researchers’ modelling, annual growth of 12 per cent in both Tesla’s share price and earnings would leave the company just short of its profits target after a decade.

If only one operational milestone was met (cumulative vehicle deliveries), Musk would get a payout of about $8 billion – a big sum, yes, but a fraction of the headline award.

However, if Tesla is acquired, the agreement completely waives the operational targets. If Tesla were taken over, the same share-price growth could deliver Musk $448 billion to $545 billion at a typical 20-30 per cent takeover premium, or up to about $707 billion at a 50 per cent takeover premium.

In other words, Musk could bag up to 88 times what he would earn on the operational track, without meeting a single operational goal.

As Tesla sales tank, Musk gains a trillion-dollar pay day

The pay deal “converts a performance award into a transaction bonus”, potentially allowing Musk to engineer a takeover through an affiliated company such as SpaceX, triggering a huge payout while bypassing the operational targets.

Perhaps Musk’s greatest feat of engineering is financial rather than technological: the salesman who persuaded more than 75 per cent of shareholders to back a pay deal that has “essentially no analogue in market practice”.

]]>Julia Demaree Nikhinson<![CDATA[A Dublin woman in Ottawa: ‘Canadians take time to adapt to our humour and way of doing business’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/25/canada-didnt-dilute-my-irish-identity-it-gave-me-the-distance-to-understand-its-value/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/25/canada-didnt-dilute-my-irish-identity-it-gave-me-the-distance-to-understand-its-value/Sun, 18 Oct 2026 08:33:58 +0000Growing up in south Co Dublin and attending school in Mount Anville, Jackie Gilna credits her father for giving her the broadest possible appreciation of Irish culture. Wherever possible, the family were exposed to their farming heritage.

“My dad was from Longford. I was that Dublin jackeen. My grandmother would say how awful it was that I was being brought up in the city, and I would be made to drink the milk from a cow. But that brought me closer to an Irish experience than I would not have experienced in Dublin.

“We were also brought all around Ireland, and my dad told me, ‘You will not leave these shores until you know every corner and you are an ambassador for your country’.”

Earlier immersion in Irish culture was a formative influence, she says, in a career that has been shaped around promoting Ireland abroad and bringing the diaspora closer. Gilna, the founder of We Are Global Irish, is on a mission to harness and grow networks of Irish communities throughout the world to support each other, places where businesses and professionals can come together to share information and help each other in practical ways.

We Are Global Irish was launched in 2024 as a private sector company complementing the work of State agencies. As well as networking and introductions, it provides a range of practical business supports and publishes a monthly online magazine called the Irish Exchange.

The business is registered in Canada and, while the largest element of the Irish diaspora is in North America, the venture has a global reach, she says.

“One thing that stands out to me was that the world we live in as the Irish abroad is very fragmented but, when you bring people together, everyone knows someone who knows somebody; there’s only a couple of degrees of separation.

“We have State agencies who do phenomenal work, such as Enterprise Ireland and IDA Ireland, for example – the envy of other countries – and we work closely with them but there needed to be something in the private sector.”

‘There are 30 Irish people in Brandon, Canada. You miss the craic living in a small place’

Gilna’s corporate career took shape in the Netherlands and later Canada, where she moved with her Canadian husband and their familyin 2000. For more than three decades she worked mainly with small and medium-sized businesses, helping them establish, structure and reshape for growth.

“The diaspora didn’t really exist in the Netherlands. It was too close to home. When you come across the pond here, however, the notion of being Irish is very different ... Canada didn’t dilute my Irish identity. It gave me the distance to understand its value, commercially and culturally.”

In a forerunner of what she was to do later, Gilna helped establish the Irish Chamber of Commerce in Ottawa at the invitation of the then ambassador and says that listening to Irish people abroad over the years gave her an understanding of their desire to contribute to Ireland.

She is very grateful to Canada for giving her the opportunity to build an independent career, build new connections, stay connected to Ireland and to add value between both countries. In this, she is in good company: some 4½ million people in Canada claim some Irish DNA, according to census data.

Asked about the current strains in relations between Canada and the United States, and prime minister Mark Carney’s desire to form closer relations with the EU, Gilna is characteristically diplomatic. She says that, ultimately, the fundamentally strong historic and good neighbourly relationship between Canada and the United States will endure but that forging closer relations with Europe also makes sense for cultural as well as more obvious economic reasons, given the strong European roots of much of the population.

‘We’re an Irish-Canadian-French household. I’m finally getting some return on my Leaving Cert French’

She and her family have enjoyed life in the Canadian capital, where the climate varies enormously. “It can get into the minus-30s in winter but with blue skies and crisp snow. A calmness comes over us in those months. In the summer we enjoy high temperatures from May to September.

“In Ottawa you can be who you are. You don’t have to blend in and be Canadian, so it’s not a melting pot and that’s a cultural difference between here and other places.”

Canadians can be risk averse and polite. There is a different style of doing business from the way it is done in Ireland, she says. Anyone doing business with Canada also needs to factor in the wide regional divergence between different parts of this vast country.

“In Ireland we operate at a fast pace and the craic comes into everything, as professional and all as we are in our engagement. However, Canadians like to take things a bit slower, and they take time to adapt to our humour and our way of doing business.”

While there are economic opportunities for Irish people wishing to find a home in Canada, she cautions anyone interested in this to do their homework thoroughly in advance, not to underestimate the challenges and, most importantly, “don’t arrive without a job”.

]]><![CDATA[How HR teams are combatting AI and other security threats in recruitment process]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/18/human-resources-doesnt-need-to-be-the-cia/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/18/human-resources-doesnt-need-to-be-the-cia/Sun, 18 Oct 2026 09:00:00 +0000What would you think if you were asked in a job interview to hold up three fingers in front of your face? Perhaps you’re doing so badly that they’re checking you’re not concussed?

More likely the recruiter is trying to check that you’re not an artificial intelligence (AI) deepfake.

Employers are trying all sorts of things to combat fraudulent AI use in the recruitment process. There are jobseekers who use chatbots to bluff their way into jobs they’re not capable of, or pay “interview mules” to complete assessments for them.

More dangerously, there are hackers who try to get hired with false identities in order to access internal systems, and even remote information technology (IT) workers who turn out to be based in North Korea. The research company Gartner has predicted that one in four candidate profiles worldwide will be fake by 2028.

All this is leading to a culture clash inside companies. The warm and fuzzy realms of human resources (HR) and recruitment are having to learn to work with the suspicious minds of the cybersecurity world.

One example: the HR platform Deel acquired AI cybersecurity company Clarity in August in order to “embed continuous identity security across the entire hiring and workforce life cycle”.

Neev Wilf, who was at Clarity and is now head of product at Deel Security, tells me that “bringing HR and security to the same room is tough” because they “have different interests”. Security teams usually want “every protection, every feature, all the way” but “at the same time, you have [recruiters] who say ‘this enhances friction for the candidate’”.

What sort of security checks are we talking about here? Recruitment platform Greenhouse has introduced a system to allow employers to prompt job seekers for ID verification. “Some do it at the top of the funnel, in the beginning of the process, and some do it further down,” Daniel Chait, Greenhouse’s chief executive, tells me.

Clarity, meanwhile, says it uses AI to examine “facial movements, lip-syncing, eye motions, voice patterns” and other indicators in video interviews, and cross-checks indicators such as “behavioural, identity, and media patterns” to spot signals of deception.

It sounds like a lot of personal data to be hoovered up in a process that might not even result in a job offer. There is surely the potential, too, for “false positives”: for legitimate candidates to be flagged as suspicious and thus denied the chance of getting hired. If a lot of employers start to use the same handful of systems, some unlucky souls might find themselves blocked again and again.

The good news is that the EU’s penchant for regulation has helped pre-empt some of these potential pitfalls. Both the General Data Protection Regulation directive and the European Union AI Act give people protection against being subject to unexplained automated decision-making, for example, especially in high-stakes areas such as recruitment.

Interviewing Gen Z teachers: A candidate told me I was in a bidding war for her

Both Wilf and Chait tell me their systems have been carefully designed to meet EU regulations and do not lead to automated decisions but only flag information for human review.

That said, these new security features and identity checks feel like a depressing consequence of the AI arms race in recruitment. Already, candidates complain they feel dehumanised by employers’ use of the technology, while employers say they can’t cope with the volume of AI-assisted applications.

According to Gartner’s regular surveys of job seekers, the number of people who had experienced an AI-led interview doubled from 9 per cent in the third quarter of last year to 18 per cent in the second quarter of this year. But only 30 per cent said they felt comfortable with the experience, only 20 per cent felt they were able to get their own questions about the job answered and only 17 per cent preferred the experience to a human interviewer.

Have we reached the point where employers throw up their hands and go back to a much smaller pool of handwritten applications and in-person interviews?

It’s an appealing thought, but it’s worth remembering that way of doing things was hardly perfect either. Indeed, perhaps the worst-case scenario would be a future that contains a bit of both.

A return to more offline, human-to-human recruitment decisions for those who already have personal connections who can vouch for them (or those young people whose parents have connections). And for job seekers without that reserve of social capital? An interview into a webcam with three fingers pressed to your face. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

]]>rudi_suardi<![CDATA[Leaving shares to a spouse at death can make more sense than a lifetime transfer ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/18/leaving-shares-to-a-spouse-at-death-can-make-more-sense-than-a-lifetime-transfer/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/18/leaving-shares-to-a-spouse-at-death-can-make-more-sense-than-a-lifetime-transfer/Sun, 18 Oct 2026 09:00:00 +0000I own shares in a company which, if sold today, would attract a large tax liability. In one of your articles, you state that “section 1028 of the Taxes Consolidation Act provides that no capital gains arises on assets that are given by one spouse to another”.

So if I transfer my shareholding into my wife’s name, I am no longer liable for capital gains tax (CGT) in that shareholding and my wife’s tax liability commences from the time she receives the shares until the time she eventually sells them. Is that correct? Is the transfer to my wife by way of a gift? Does gift tax arise?

Does the share transfer require new share certificates to be issued in my wife’s name? If so, is this a simple matter? Are there any fees involved in such a transfer?

In the event of my wife’s death, these shares would become part of her estate and would not attract CGT. Is that right?

I understand from your article that if my wife died before me and she left the shares to me, I would again be liable to large capital gains liability. Should my wife indicate in her will that these shares should pass to my daughter, would this resolve the above issue?

DS

Investing in individual stocks is clearly a high-risk game as all your eggs are in one basket rather than being diversified across a number of shares or other assets in an exchange trade fund (ETF). However, stock markets have enjoyed a very strong run in recent years and, for those who chose wisely (or fortunately), their investments have secured strong gains.

And that raises the issue of tax planning.

None of us wants to pay any more tax than we are required to and, as that recent letter to which you refer highlighted, there are potentially valuable exemptions that can help couples do this.

When budget changes kick in and how to claim them

Irish law determines that gifts (and inheritances) between spouses do not attract any capital acquisitions tax (CAT) liability. So anything your wife gives you or you give your wife is exempt from this tax, which is more commonly known as inheritance tax or gift tax.

You ask whether the transfer you are considering would be seen as a gift? It will, yes, but not one that is liable for gift tax.

At a practical level, you sensibly raise the issue of share certificates or, in more recent times, an electronic record of share ownership.

Registrars are companies that manage the share registers of listed companies. Most particularly, they keep track of who owns how many shares and record changes of ownership when shares are sold or otherwise transferred.

They also keep shareholders notified of company events, such as annual meetings, share placings, rights issues, consolidation, or special meetings to approve things like takeovers, etc.

There are a number of companies that specialise in this work. You do not identify which company’s shares we are talking about here so I cannot tell you which one you need to approach, but the information will be readily available in the investor relations section of the website of the company you’ve invested in.

You can also get the details from any email or letter they may have sent you.

They will send you a share transfer form to formalise the transfer of ownership of these shares to your wife. There will be a charge to do this. I cannot say precisely how much this will be but it tends to be fairly nominal.

If you do not have your share certificate, things can get a bit more costly as you may need to sign (and pay for) an indemnity letter.

The whole thing is a fairly straightforward process though it can be slightly bureaucratic and stressful for people unused to dealing with share registrars, a group which, by the nature of their work, tends to communicate in fairly formal legal terms.

Capital gains tax

But what about CGT? By your own admission, you have built up quite a CGT liability on these shares over time.

This was the gist of the previous question and, as I said then, the transfer to your wife does not trigger any CGT bill. However, that does not mean that the capital gain you have made disappears; it just transfers to your wife.

While neither of you has any tax bill to pay right now, your wife is deemed to have acquired the shares not on the date you transfer them to her and at their price on that day, but on the date and at the price you originally acquired them for.

If she sells them down the line, all you have really done is transfer your large CGT bill to her.

But what about if she holds them until she dies? Well then, as I said in response to the previous query, the capital gain will die with her. Any capital gain dies with the owner of an asset.

Whoever succeeds her in owning these shares will not have to worry about the legacy capital gain dating back to the time you originally acquired the shares. The only capital gain that will apply for new owners will be the difference in the price when your wife dies and the price at which they eventually sell the shares.

This, as another reader found recently, can create unexpected tax liability as probate generally takes a year and, in strong equity markets, people can find themselves unwittingly with an outstanding capital gain the moment they actually get access to shares. For the new owner, capital gains does not start with when they get control of the shares but when the previous owner dies.

Inheritance tax reform could unlock €170bn sitting on deposit, expert says

There is one area where you appear to have confused something I have mentioned previously. You understand that if your wife were to leave the shares to you when she dies, the clock goes back to when you originally bought these shares. That is not so.

If your wife were to subsequently transfer the shares back to you while alive, yes, that is the case. But not if she leaves them to you in her will or even in the absence of a will.

Whether your wife leaves these shares to you, her daughter, or anyone else, no CGT issue arises. She can mention them specifically in her will, she can simply leave them to be dealt with under a residuary clause – a clause all wills should have dealing with assets not otherwise allocated to a specific beneficiary – or they can be dealt with under intestacy. In none of those cases will capital gains arise, even if she leaves them to you.

What may arise is our old friend CAT.

Anything your wife leaves you in her will or anything you otherwise inherit from her is free of inheritance tax but that is not the case for her daughter or any other beneficiary.

The budget raised the amounts anyone can receive in inheritance without paying tax. For a child inheriting from a parent, this threshold is now €420,000. That will cover anything your daughter inherits from either parent and also any gift they may have received from you in your lifetimes over the value of €3,000 in any one year.

But at the end of all this, I have one question for you?

If the intention is not to sell the shares, why bother with this lifetime transfer? If you sell the shares or you transfer them to your wife and she sells them, the same CGT bill arises – and in most families will be paid from the common family financial pool.

And if either of you dies owning the shares, no CGT applies.

Inheritance tax in Ireland: ‘The rules are absolutely skewed against the childless’

The only real financial benefit here is if your wife dies before you, having taken ownership of the shares, and then leaves them to you in her will. That would wipe out your CGT liability for sure.

But demographics suggest that a woman will live longer than a man in Ireland, even these days. And it would seem to benefit her more when considering tax exposure to receive these shares from you via your will when she does not have to worry about any tax bill – CGT or CAT.

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3444974/">
   <title>Sprache als „Axt“, Literatur als Gedächtnis</title>
   <description>Spätestens mit dem Roman „Die Klavierspielerin“ (1983), der von Michael Haneke 2001 verfilmt wurde, ist Elfriede Jelinek zu einer der bekanntesten und streitbarsten Schriftstellerinnen im deutschsprachigen Raum avanciert. Wesentliche Themen ihres Werks sind bis heute die herrschenden Geschlechterverhältnisse, der Kapitalismus und die Kontinuität faschistischer Tendenzen in der Gesellschaft. 2004 wurde ihr der Literaturnobelpreis zuerkannt. Am Dienstag feiert Jelinek ihren 80. Geburtstag.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3445519/">
   <title>Unis stellen sich auf Personalabbau ein</title>
   <description>Die Universitätenkonferenz (uniko) hat erneut ihren Unmut über das von der Regierung präsentierte Budget für die Universitäten geäußert. Bei einer Pressekonferenz am Montag wurde infolge der Budgetpläne ein Personalabbau im Ausmaß von mindestens zehn Prozent angekündigt. Der Regierung warf die uniko angesichts der Darstellung der Budgetzahlen ein Schönrechnen der Beträge vor. Wissenschaftsministerin Eva-Maria Holzleitner (SPÖ) hatte das Unibudget am Sonntag verteidigt. Für Donnerstag wurde wieder zu Protesten aufgerufen.</description>

Poland has detained and expelled 15 Russians and Belarusians who tried to take part in youth world karate championships that were taking place in the Polish city of Bielsko-Biała.

“Eleven Belarusian citizens and four Russians entered the country on tourist visas, which was inconsistent with the declared purpose of their stay in Poland,” said border guard spokesman Szymon Mościcki.

After being detained, they received orders to leave the country within eight days, which is “the shortest possible deadline”, he added, quoted by broadcaster TVP.

Piętnastu obywateli Rosji i Białorusi zostało zatrzymanych przez Straż Graniczną. Przyjechali do Polski na wizach turystycznych, choć prawdopodobnie zamierzali wziąć udział w mistrzostwach świata w karate. Otrzymali decyzje nakazujące opuszczenie kraju.https://t.co/czcjQKZ2kw

— tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 19, 2026

The announcement came one day after the karate world championships in the cadet, junior and U-21 categories had finished in Bielsko-Biała.

In early October, Russia’s TASS news agency had reported that some of the country’s junior karatekas, as competitors are known, had planned to compete in the tournament. The World Karate Federation (WKF) allows Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete under a neutral banner.

However, Poland has a strict policy of not allowing Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete in tournaments on its territory. This year, it banned them from taking part in a World Cup ski jumping event. It was also removed as host of two European junior weightlifting championships for banning Russian and Belarusian athletes.

 

On 15 October, the day after the championships in Bielsko-Biała had started, TASS reported that none of the Russian athletes had been allowed to register by the Polish organisers.

Paweł Połtorzecki, president of the Polish Karate Union (PUK), confirmed that, despite PUK warning them not to come, Russian and Belarusian athletes had sought to take part, prompting the organisers to ask the border guard to conduct an inspection.

“The first sign was the appearance of a Russian at the refereeing course,” he revealed, quoted by TVP. “That’s when the first detention occurred.”

Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading Polish daily, reports that the Russian karatekas had obtained tourist visas from other countries in the European Schengen area, of which Poland is part. Poland itself does not issue tourist visas to Russians.

Poland has been removed as the host of two European junior weightlifting championships after refusing to allow Russian athletes to take part

The European Weightlifting Federation says it "does not accept discrimination based on geopolitical circumstances" https://t.co/j7PfiTHZ1M

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 9, 2026

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has been one of Kyiv’s closest allies, providing military and humanitarian support while also pressing for tougher international sanctions against Moscow.

Meanwhile, Poland has become the primary target in Europe for sabotage operations carried out by operatives working on behalf of Russia, including arson attacks and an attempt to derail a train. Russia has also repeatedly violated Polish airspace with drones, missiles and, most recently, a helicopter.

In response to Russia’s aggressive actions, Poland has successively shut down all Russian consulates on its territory. Moscow responded by likewise closing all Polish consulates that it previously hosted. In January, Russia warned its citizens against travelling to Poland due to “Russophobia”.

Poland says it has broken up an international criminal group responsible for laundering an estimated 337 million zloty (€77 million) by using currency exchange offices to illegally process money obtained from internet scams.

Nine suspects – eight Ukrainians and one Belarusian – have been detained in a series of raids, which also resulted in the seizure of gold and cash worth over 1 million zloty.

Służby rozbiły międzynarodową grupę zajmującą się praniem pieniędzy z oszustw inwestycyjnych i kryptowalut. Zatrzymano 9 osób, a skala transakcji przekroczyła 337 mln zł. Zabezpieczono złoto i gotówkę wartą ponad 1 mln zł. @Straz_Graniczna @PolicjaCBZC @ABW_GOV_PL pic.twitter.com/g2NQoqaPvP

— Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) October 19, 2026

The accused – four women and five men aged between 26 and 53 – were arrested in Łódź, Warsaw and Małopolska province, announced Krzysztof Kopania, spokesman for the Łódź regional prosecutor’s office, which is leading the investigation.

The detainees are four female cashiers, three men running the exchange offices, and two couriers used to transport money. All have been charged with participating in an organised criminal group and money laundering. They could face up to 15 years in prison if convicted.

Prosecutors say that the gang, which operated in the cities of Warsaw, Lublin, Wrocław, Katowice and Gdańsk, collected money that had been obtained through internet fraud and transported it to cryptocurrency exchanges. It was then processed without complying with anti-money laundering procedures.

Proceeds were then transferred to bank accounts, sent abroad by car, or concealed in fictitious purchases of gold. Most money was ultimately invested in cryptocurrencies.

 

“The scale of the operation was enormous,” said Kopania. “It is estimated that between February 2025 and July 2026, members of the group took steps to conceal the origins of approximately 337 million zloty.”

The ringleader was a 34-year-old Ukrainian national who made the key decisions and oversaw the domestic and international channelling of funds obtained from illegal sources, according to the Internal Security Agency (ABW) and border guard, which were also involved in the operation.

Seven of the accused have been placed in pre-trial detention for three (or in one case two) months, while two have been bailed and ordered not to leave Poland.

This article has been updated to include a statement from Poland’s defence ministry issued on Monday afternoon.

Lithuania says there is “no doubt” that a Ukrainian drone which exploded on its territory on Sunday, hitting a moving car, entered its airspace from Poland. However, Poland has so far said that there is no confirmation of an object crossing the border.

Meanwhile, Ukraine has apologised for the incident, saying that Russian electronic warfare had diverted the drone’s path during an operation against military targets in Russia.

Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and EU.

This morning, NATO fighter jets stationed at Šiauliai Air Base scrambled once again after an unidentified object entered Lithuanian airspace.

What appears to be a drone exploded…

— Gitanas Nausėda (@GitanasNauseda) October 18, 2026

On Sunday morning, Lithuania confirmed that a drone had entered its airspace and exploded, causing damage to a moving vehicle. NATO jets were scrambled in response to the incursion but were not able to visually identify the object.

President Gitanas Nausėda said that the incident was further evidence that “Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and [the] EU”.

Meanwhile, Lithuanian defence minister Robertas Kaunas revealed that preliminary information indicated the drone had entered from Polish airspace.

“I have already contacted the Polish defence minister and asked Poland to join the investigation so that we can look into this incident together,” said Kaunas, quoted by broadcaster LRT.

 

However, a spokesman for Poland’s defence ministry, Janusz Sejmej, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) on Sunday that “there is no confirmation [from our radar systems] of [an object] crossing the border from Poland to Lithuania”.

Polsat, a leading Polish broadcaster, cited unnamed sources at Poland’s defence ministry saying that they believed the drone in fact took off from within Lithuanian territory, around 30 kilometres from the Polish border, and then flew deep into the country.

In response, Deividas Matulionis, an advisor to the Lithuanian president, told the Baltic News Service (BNS) on Monday that “I can say very unequivocally we have credible evidence that the drone crossed the Polish border”.

Later, the country’s prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, said that “there is no doubt that it entered…from the Polish side”. He also confirmed that the evidence indicates the drone “is of Ukrainian origin”.

We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia.

We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have…

— Heorhii Tykhyi (@SpoxUkraineMFA) October 18, 2026

Those remarks followed a statement on Sunday afternoon from Heorhii Tykhyi, the spokesman for Ukraine’s foreign ministry, who appeared to confirm that the drone was Ukrainian.

“We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia,” wrote Tykhyi. “We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have caused.”

The spokesman said that Ukraine would “share all relevant information with our Lithuanian partners to establish the full circumstances of the incident”. However, he gave no further information on what type of drone was involved, where it was launched from, and what its target was.

Lithuania borders Belarus, an ally of Russia, and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, as well as Poland and Latvia. In March and May this year, a number of Ukrainian drones aimed at targets in Russia entered the airspaces of NATO members Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia and Finland, likely due to Russian electronic jamming.

On Monday afternoon, Poland’s defence ministry issued a statement “strongly refuting” media reports suggesting that sources within the ministry had identified the drone as having taken off within Lithuania itself.

It added that the ministry, in cooperation with its Lithuanian partners, was still “conducting a detailed analysis” of what had taken place.

Poland has condemned an attack by masked Israeli settlers on a delegation of European diplomats – including Polish ones – that was visiting the West Bank.

It called for a “decisive response from the Israeli authorities”, saying that the incident is “further evidence of the settler violence that the Palestinian population in the West Bank faces on a daily basis”.

The attack has likewise been condemned by France and Belgium, whose nationals were also in the delegation, and the European Union, as well as by the Israeli foreign minister.

Masked Israeli settlers attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, prompting European condemnation.

The violence comes amid unprecedented settler pogroms during the olive harvest. pic.twitter.com/wsP6edL62y

— Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) October 18, 2026

On Saturday, the delegation – which included members from France, Belgium and Poland as well as representatives of the Catholic church – visited the mostly Christian Palestinian village of Taybeh near Ramallah in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.

They had come to assess the situation following regular recent attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to harvest olives on their own land. During the visit, the delegation came under attack, with parts of the incident caught on camera.

France’s foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, reported that Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France, had been “violently assaulted” during the incident. He demanded that Israel arrest the perpetrators and “urgently put an end to these criminal acts of violence”.

 

Late on Saturday afternoon, the spokesman for Poland’s foreign ministry, Maciej Wewiór, issued a statement confirming that the attack had taken place and that the delegation had included an unspecified number of Polish diplomats, who he said had not been harmed.

“We express our deep outrage and strongly condemn this incident,” added Wewiór. “Poland consistently opposes violence by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank. Attacks on representatives of the diplomatic corps are absolutely unacceptable.”

The spokesman said that Poland now “expects urgent and detailed explanations from the Israeli authorities” and for the perpetrators of the attack to be identified and held accountable. “We also expect effective measures to prevent similar incidents in the future.”

❗Potwierdzamy, że na Zachodnim Brzegu Jordanu doszło do ataku na konwój, w którym znajdowali się przedstawiciele korpusu dyplomatycznego, w tym polscy dyplomaci. Według wstępnych informacji za atak mogą odpowiadać izraelscy osadnicy.
Polskim dyplomatom nic się nie stało. Z…

— Rzecznik MSZ – Maciej Wewiór (@RzecznikMSZ) October 17, 2026

On Sunday, Poland’s foreign ministry issued a further statement in which it “condemned the attack by masked settlers…during a solidarity visit to a town known for its centuries-old Christian presence”.

The incident “is further evidence of the settler violence that the Palestinian population in the West Bank faces on a daily basis”, they added, calling for a “decisive response from the Israeli authorities”.

The attack was also “strongly condemned” on Sunday by the European Union’s diplomatic service, which said that it “expects full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians”.

Belgium’s foreign minister, Maxime Prevot, said that his country would continue to “press for EU sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them”.

🇵🇸 I condemn in the strongest terms the attack by masked settlers in Taybeh, in the occupied West Bank, against Palestinians, our Consul General, French and Polish diplomats as well as catholic representatives. A French mayor was assaulted and a Belgian vehicle damaged. Our team…

— Maxime PREVOT (@prevotmaxime) October 17, 2026

In the wake of the incident, Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu had urged people to show “caution before drawing conclusions” over what had happened. He claimed that there is “a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents” of the West Bank.

However, the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said that it “strongly condemns the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters”. But it added that “the consulate’s visit was not coordinated with the IDF”, which is “important to prevent incidents of this kind”.

Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, also issued a condemnation of the attack and said that police had opened an investigation.

The IDF strongly condemns the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters.

Police forces and forensic investigators from the Judea and Samaria District are entering the area accompanied by…

— Israel Defense Forces (@IDF) October 17, 2026

The incident involving the diplomatic group came a day after around 80 Israeli settlers had attacked Palestinians harvesting olives, with Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine among those injured.

Levine told the Committee to Protect Journalists, an American non-profit organisation, that she had been pushed to the ground by a group of masked settlers, who “were kicking me for I think at least 10 minutes”.

That incident prompted criticism of Israel from the United States, whose ambassador, Mike Huckabee, called it a “despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards”.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, said he was “disturbed” by the incident and confirmed that “we’ve asked the Israelis to crack down on that”.

.@SecRubio on reporter Heidi Levine being attacked in the West Bank: "We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing….the President has been very clear, he's said this repeatedly, he does not want to see friction or crisis going on in the West Bank." pic.twitter.com/Xg10vteeXK

— CSPAN (@cspan) October 18, 2026

In August this year, Poland summoned Israel’s ambassador to express its “great disappointment” that the IDF had discontinued an investigation into the strikes on an aid convoy in Gaza in 2024 that killed seven humanitarian workers, including a Pole, Damian Soból.

In May, Poland issued a five-year entry ban on Israeli national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir for his treatment of detained activists, including Polish citizens, from a flotilla seeking to reach Gaza.

Last year, Israel criticised Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, after he suggested that Israeli politicians are causing the starvation of mothers and children in Gaza. The Israeli foreign ministry called the remarks “unacceptable” and urged Tusk to “remember the lessons” of the Holocaust.

]]> Poland moves to allow more municipalities to charge tourist fee https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/17/poland-moves-to-allow-more-municipalities-to-charge-tourist-fee/ Sat, 17 Oct 2026 10:37:35 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105619
