Many more municipalities in Poland will be allowed to charge a daily fee for tourists and other overnight visitors after a change to the law dropping environmental requirements for levying such charges.

Kraków, which received 8.7 million overnight tourists last year, had in particular been pushing for the change. However, Poland as a whole has seen a recent boom in visitor numbers, recording the EU’s second-fastest growth in the number of nights in tourist accommodation last year.

#Krakow #opłataturystyczna #ustawa 🚨🔥Z OSTATNIEJ CHWILI! 🔥🚨

📢 Prezydent RP podpisał nowelizację przepisów dotyczących podatków i opłat lokalnych, PIT oraz PCC.

🏨 Najważniejsze zmiany dla branży turystycznej dotyczą opłaty miejscowej i uzdrowiskowej.

🗓️ Od 2027 r. za jej… pic.twitter.com/9ATvENvNol

— Kraków (@krakow_pl) October 15, 2026

Until now, a “visitor’s fee” could be levied by municipalities with beneficial climatic features, “scenic qualities” and the capacity to accommodate people visiting to benefit from these attributes, as well as localities in areas with the status of a “spa protection area”. In practice, this largely applied to seaside and mountain resorts.

Kraków did charge a visitor’s fee between 2004 and 2015, but was subsequently unable to do so due to a toughening of environmental requirements. The city has long suffered from bad air pollution, though it has taken significant steps to tackle the issue.

Now, under new legislation proposed by the government earlier this year and signed into law by President Karol Nawrocki this week, the requirement for beneficial climatic features has been scrapped, meaning many more places will be able to charge the visitor’s fee.

 

From 1 January, municipalities with scenic qualities will be able to charge visitors up to 5 zloty (€1.14) for each night they stay in hotels, guesthouses and short-term rental accommodation for up to one month, a rise on the current maximum of 3.46 zloty.

Additionally, whereas previously only people visiting for the purposes of tourism had to pay, the fee now applies to all visits, including for work or health purposes, reports broadcaster TVN. People with significant disabilities, children with certified disabilities and their carers will be exempt from the fee.

In another change, fees will be collected directly by accommodation providers, who will be required to maintain detailed records, reports the Infor news service. Passing fees on in a timely manner will entitle providers to receive at least 10% of the money they collect.

Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026

In 2024, Kraków appealed to the government to be allowed to charge tourists a fee, noting that “overtourism leads to tensions and social discontent”, as the “local community suffers” and “residents increasingly feel like tourists in their own city”.

With its UNESCO-listed Old Town, Wawel royal castle, and former Jewish district of Kazimierz, Kraków is regularly named as one of Europe’s best tourist destinations. Last year, a record 16.25 million people visited the city, of whom 8.7 million stayed overnight.

While that is a boon to the local economy, it also often causes tensions with residents, who complain about noise and disruption. In 2024, the city created the new position of “night mayor”, whose role is to reconcile the needs of tourists, businesses and residents.

Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals of the type offered through services such as Airbnb.

Such accommodation has boomed in recent years, often prompting a backlash from local residents https://t.co/8MRfRWTDxd

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 3, 2026

Following this week’s change to the law, Kraków city hall confirmed that it would now again be able to collect a visitor’s fee “if the statutory conditions are satisfied and the municipal council adopts an appropriate resolution”.

The city’s recently elected new mayor, Łukasz Gibała, who will be sworn in next week, said before Sunday’s election that he was in favour of a tourist tax of at least 20 zloty per night, four times the new maximum.

“In western European cities there are rates of that size and higher,” Gibała said, quoted by financial news service Money.pl. “Maintaining the city in the face of the influx of tourists is costly. In Kraków, private business owners profit from tourism, whilst the city and its residents foot the bill.”

Poland as a whole has also experienced a boom in tourism. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-largest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation. Its increase of 7% was behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta (9.9%).

]]> Poland drops proposal to criminalise providing help to illegal migrants following outcry https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/16/poland-drops-proposal-to-criminalise-providing-help-to-illegal-migrants-following-outcry/ Fri, 16 Oct 2026 14:38:51 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105617

Poland’s interior ministry has withdrawn a proposal to make it a criminal offence, punishable by up to three years in prison, to provide support to migrants who are in the country illegally. The idea had prompted criticism from human rights groups and even opposition from within the government.

The interior ministry said the amendment had been intended to clamp down on migrant smuggling. But activists feared it would criminalise humanitarian aid, such as that provided to migrants who have irregularly crossed the border from Belarus.

Za udzielenie bezinteresownej pomocy migrantom nie będzie groziła kara do trzech lat więzienia. Po burzy, którą wywołała publikacja „Rzeczpospolitej” i po sprzeciwie resortu rodziny, MSWiA wycofuje się z pomysłu „karania za podanie posiłku”.https://t.co/Q0N52IMRVn

— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 15, 2026

Under current Polish law, anyone who facilitates the illegal stay of a person in Poland in exchange for financial or personal benefit can be jailed for up to five years.

However, this week, the interior ministry proposed an amendment that would also have penalised anyone who knowingly “enabled or facilitated” the illegal stay of someone in Poland, even if not for financial or personal benefit. The offence would have been punishable by up to three years in prison.

“Currently, this behaviour is not criminalised, creating a loophole for those who exploit such situations and, under the pretext of helping migrants, aid them in their illegal stay, thus serving as a springboard for further illegal migration,” wrote deputy interior minister Czesław Mroczek, quoted by the Rzeczpospolita daily.

 

That immediately prompted concern that the law could be used against volunteers and residents of border areas who provide aid – such as food, water, medical treatment, clothing or shelter – to migrants who have crossed illegally from Belarus.

Since 2021, tens of thousands of people, mainly from Asia and Africa, have tried to cross that border with the encouragement and support of the Belarusian authorities. They have sometimes used violence against Polish border officers.

Poland and the EU accuse Belarus of “weaponising” migration as part of the “hybrid warfare” being waged by Russia and its allies against European countries. They have implemented tough border protection measures to prevent crossings and facilitate “pushbacks” of those who cross.

However, many human rights and aid organisations argue that the migrants – over 100 of whom have died around the border since 2021 – are often victims of this process and need humanitarian support.

By Daniel Tilles

Poland will hold parliamentary elections a year from now. The outcome will decide who governs the country for the next four years – although, given how close the polls are, and with questions over coalition formation, it could also result in uncertainty, chaos, and even new elections being called.

Below, we explain how the elections work, which parties will be standing, what kind of outcomes are possible, and which issues may animate the campaign.

When will the election take place?

Assuming early elections are not called, the vote must take place on a non-working day in the last 30 days before the end of the current four-year parliamentary term, which began on 13 November 2023.

Because elections in Poland are held on Sundays, that gives four possible dates: 17, 24 or 31 October, or 7 November (though 1 November and 11 November, which are public holidays, are also theoretically possible).

It is the president, Karol Nawrocki, who will choose the date. He must do so no later than 90 days before the end of the current parliamentary term.

How does voting work?

The 460 members of the more powerful lower house, the Sejm, are elected through proportional representation, meaning that seats are distributed more or less on the basis of the share of the vote parties receive (using the so-called D’Hondt method for allocating seats from electoral lists put forward by each party). However, parties must receive at least 5% of the vote nationally to enter parliament (a figure that rises to 8% for coalitions of parties who stand on a single electoral list).

The 100 members of the upper-house Senate are chosen through a first-past-the-post system similar to how members of the US Congress or British House of Commons are elected, with the candidate in each district that receives the most votes winning the seat.

How is a government formed?

A government can only be formed if it can win a vote of confidence in the Sejm.

After the elections, the president designates a prime minister, who is tasked with forming a government – which would almost certainly be made up of a coalition of parties – that must then win a vote of confidence.

If they fail to do so (as happened in 2023), the Sejm votes to choose an alternative prime minister, who likewise must try to form a government that has the confidence of the Sejm.

Parliament has chosen @donaldtusk as Poland's new prime minister.

That paves the way for him to form a new government in the coming days, ending the eight-year rule of the national-conservative PiS party https://t.co/iZUKh2rxnP

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 11, 2023

If that fails, the president has a second chance to pick a prime minister, who must again win a confidence vote. However, whereas the previous two votes require an absolute majority (większość bezwzględna) to be carried, this time only a simple majority is needed, making it easier to form a minority government.

If this third and final attempt does not work, then parliament is dissolved and new elections are called.

Who is likely to form the next government?

At the moment, it is incredibly difficult to say. Polls suggest an even split in support between parties generally aligned with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition – which ranges from left to centre right – and the right-wing opposition. However, the 5% electoral threshold complicates the picture.

According to current polling averages compiled by Polish website eWybory and Politico Europe, Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) leads with 32%. One of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), is on 7%, while two others, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), are on around 3% and 1%, respectively. Another left-wing party, Together (Razem), which previously caucused with the ruling coalition but split in 2024, is on around 4%.

Meanwhile, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, is on 20%. Two far-right opposition groups, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have 14% and 9%, respectively. The right-wing Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which broke away from PiS this year, is at around 5%.

Rolling 30-day average support in polls for Poland’s main political parties (source: eWybory.eu)

If we treat those as two potential blocs, parties more or less aligned with the current government are on around 47% while the right-wing opposition is on 48%. However, PSL and Poland 2050 currently look likely to fall below the 5% threshold if they stand alone, meaning votes for them would not count. That would significantly harm Tusk’s chances of forming a new government. If Rozwój Plus stood alone and fell below the threshold, that would harm the opposition.

It is therefore likely that, as the elections draw nearer, parties that seem likely to fall below 5% will seek to join forces with other groups. In 2023, PSL and Poland 2050 stood together in the so-called Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance. But they have made clear they do not intend to do that again. That leaves them with limited options. They could join forces with KO on a single electoral list, but that does not guarantee that their voters will follow them. Indeed, some may baulk at voting for Tusk’s party.

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026

Meanwhile, there are some wildcards in the pack. KKP, led by radical-right extremist Grzegorz Braun, is shunned by the mainstream right for its antisemitism, anti-Americanism and sympathy towards Russia. PiS’s leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, has declared that he would not allow Braun to join government. Development Plus has taken a similar position. Both parties value relations with the US and the Trump administration, whose ambassador to Poland has reportedly pushed them to rule out working with Braun.

However, if KKP maintains its current level of support, it looks almost impossible for the opposition to form a parliamentary majority without it, meaning there would be a strong temptation to somehow work with Braun. Kaczyński’s determination to remove Tusk from power may outweigh his dislike of Braun and desire to keep the Americans onside.

The Together party – if it manages to pass the 5% threshold – could likewise represent a challenge for Tusk when forming a coalition, given that it has criticised the government for failing to keep promises on healthcare spending, public sector pay, and liberalising the abortion law.

 

There also remains the possibility of some elements from each camp joining the other side – either entire parties or individual MPs defecting – in order to help form a government.

PiS has long sought to tempt PSL to its side (and recent reports suggest that even President Donald Trump tried to persuade PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, to do so). It is conceivable that Rozwój Plus could work with parts of the current ruling camp, though its hatred of Tusk would make that very difficult.

All of the difficulties outlined above mean there is a significant chance that it will not be possible for anyone to form a government, necessitating fresh elections – something that has never happened before in Poland. If that happens, it would mean uncertainty and a lack of clear leadership at a time when Poland is facing major security challenges and a worsening fiscal situation.

What about the Senate?

The Senate, like the Sejm, is currently controlled by the ruling coalition. Indeed, Tusk has an even larger majority there than in the lower house, making it harder for the opposition to flip. Although the Senate is much weaker than the Sejm – and control of it does not determine who forms the government – it does have some powers that make it a useful asset.

It can slow down the passage of legislation, though not block it. The Senate also must approve the appointment of certain officials, such as the heads of the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) and the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), as well as the Commissioner for Human Rights (RPO).

In a rare clash between Poland’s two houses of parliament, in both of which the government has a majority, the Senate has rejected a candidate chosen by the Sejm to become the new head of the state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) https://t.co/QUsqfDNh4s

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026

The upper house is also required to approve proposals by the president to hold national referendums. This year, the Senate has twice blocked moves by Nawrocki to hold a referendum on EU climate policies.

In a situation where Tusk’s coalition controlled the Sejm, and was therefore still in government, but the right-wing opposition held the Senate, that would give the president a powerful tool to call referendums on policies important to him and the opposition.

To that end, there have been calls for the right-wing and far-right opposition to form a so-called Senate pact, of the type that Tusk and his allies used to win control of the upper house in 2019 and 2023.

What that means in practice is that the parties forming the pact agree to stand only one candidate between them in each of the 100 Senate districts, making it more likely that they will scoop up votes from supporters of all the parties in the pact and win the winner-takes-all contest.

What role will Nawrocki play in all of this?

Presidents are in theory expected to be non-partisan. In practice, however, they will seek to boost parties or coalitions aligned with them, and with whom it will be easier to work.

Since Nawrocki was elected last year, relations and cooperation between the president and government have reached unprecedently low levels. Within just 10 months, Nawrocki had vetoed more bills than any previous president in history over their entire terms. He has made it abundantly clear that he would prefer to work with a government formed from the right-wing opposition.

During his first year, President Nawrocki has transformed his office into a centre of resistance to the government and become a unifying figure for the fragmented right.

However, the extent to which he will be involved in the election campaign is unclear. Some figures on the right hope that Nawrocki will act as a figurehead, using his positive relations with parties across the right-wing opposition to bring them together.

In practical terms, this could involve him acting as the patron of a Senate pact (something the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet recently said the president was willing to do), as well as helping right-wing parties form a coalition government after the elections.

Nawrocki also continues to enjoy strong approval ratings among the conservative electorate, meaning that his presence during the election campaign could act as a boost for the opposition.

What issues are likely to feature in the campaign?

A major issue will be the question of sovereignty. The right-wing opposition accuses Tusk of being Brussels’ and Berlin’s lapdog, handing over ever more power to the EU and prioritising Germany’s interests over Poland’s.

The ruling coalition, meanwhile, argues that PiS is too beholden to the Trump administration and warns that the opposition is pushing Poland towards “Polexit” from the EU, which would leave the country isolated and vulnerable, as well as much poorer.

Those battle lines extend to security policy too, with the Tusk government shifting emphasis towards Europe as a defence partner but PiS insisting that only the US can truly guarantee Poland’s security. Poland’s desire to host a new permanent US military base has already become highly politicised. If progress stalls, the opposition will blame the government. If Washington confirms that the base will go ahead, Nawrocki will seek to take the credit, based on his good relationship with Trump.

On this point, though, it is worth noting the split within the opposition. While PiS and Rozwój Plus are strongly pro-American, Confederation and, to an even greater extent, KKP, are opposed to a greater US presence in Poland.

President @NawrockiKn says that a planned new permanent US military base in Poland is “confirmed” because his American counterpart, Donald Trump, is “famous for keeping his word”.

He also suggested that the new facility will be called “Fort Trump” https://t.co/uGGJSBe5nr

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 23, 2026

Where the right-wing opposition has been united, however, is on pushing for a tougher position towards Ukraine and Ukrainian refugees in Poland.

While tensions have calmed significantly since the crisis sparked in May by President Volodymyr Zelensky naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two, it is likely that relations with Ukraine and the large-scale presence of Ukrainians in Poland will remain important issues during the election campaign.

The ruling coalition, meanwhile, will be keen to emphasise its tough overall approach to immigration, which it says was out of control under the former PiS government. It can point to the falling number of new residence permits being issued, the growing number of deportations, and tougher measures on the Belarus border, including a ban on asylum claims.

Poland has forcibly removed 2,100 foreigners from the country this year, around twice as many as in 2024.

The figures come after the government introduced a tougher new migration policy last year, which has included more deportations of foreign criminals https://t.co/zOBxPLipy8

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 31, 2025

The economy, public finances and cost of living are also likely to be major issues.

As long as the current global energy crisis sparked by the conflict around Iran continues, the opposition will seek to place the blame for record fuel prices on the government. They will also cite large deficits and the ballooning public debt as evidence that Tusk is mismanaging the economy.

The ruling coalition will point to continued strong economic growth and blame Nawrocki, who has vetoed revenue-generating tax bills, for the fiscal situation.

In one of his first policy announcements since being elected on Sunday, the new mayor of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has declared that he will withdraw official patronage of its annual LGBT+ equality march.

Łukasz Gibała, who has been supportive of LGBT+ rights in the past and has previously attended the march, argues that the event has become too “partisan”. He stood for election as an independent and has pledged to depoliticise city hall.

His decision does not prevent the march from taking place. But it means that it no longer has the official support of the city.

Kraków’s equality march, which was first held in 2004, draws thousands of participants when it takes place each year in May. The event is used to demand greater LGBT+ rights in Poland, which is ranked as one of the worst countries in Europe for LGBT+ people.

In 2021, the city’s former mayor, Jacek Majchrowski, became an honorary patron of the march. In 2024, his successor, Aleksander Miszalski, became the first mayor to attend the event, declaring that Kraków should be “a home for everyone”.

However, Miszalski was removed from office earlier this year in a recall referendum, necessitating a new election, which was won by Gibała. He beat Monika Piątkowska, who, like Miszaski, is a member of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Kraków's new mayor has announced that he will attend the city’s LGBT parade next week, something his long-serving predecessor never did.

"I want to build a tolerant Kraków, a home for everyone," says @OlekMiszalski, who took office this week https://t.co/ZQ9SzZiHp4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 9, 2024

The day after his victory, Gibała was asked by local broadcaster Radio Kraków if he would continue city hall’s patronage of the equality march. The new mayor, who takes office next week, declared that he would not, saying he “will avoid sponsoring events that have a partisan character”.

“I have the impression that, over the past three years or so, the community that organises equality marches has simply become partisan,” said Gibała. “These are people who ran for parliament and local government on the lists of specific political parties.”

Gibała did not indicate who he was referring to. However, one of the organisers of the equality march in Kraków is Magdalena Dropek, who has three times stood as a candidate for The Left (Lewica), one of the groups in Tusk’s ruling coalition, in elections to the Polish and European parliaments.

 

Gibała emphasised that he has himself attended equality marches in the past “and does not regret it”. He was previously an MP for both KO (when it was known as Civic Platform, PO) as well as for the liberal Palikot’s Movement (Ruch Palikota), later known as Your Movement (Twój Ruch).

During the recent mayoral election campaign, Gibała told broadcaster TVN that, as an MP, he had supported the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships in Poland, and said that his views had not changed.

When asked if that meant that, as mayor, he would continue the city’s practice of transcribing foreign same-sex marriages into the civil registry – as Poland was ordered to do last year by the Court of Justice of the European Union – Gibała said that he would.

In fact, although the current government supports recognition of foreign-same sex marraiges, it has not changed the law in that regard. Polish law still does not recognise any form of same-sex union.

The government, aware that opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki would veto any change to the law, instead issued a regulation (which does not require presidential approval) empowering local authorities to transcribe foreign same-sex marriages into their registries.

Many municipalities, especially more liberal larger cities, have begun to do so (some even did before the regulation was issued). But others, especially in more conservative places, have refused to, often arguing that there are legal doubts around the issue.

Data provided to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) by the digital affairs ministry last week showed that 516 foreign same-sex marriages have so far been registered in Poland. The largest numbers were in Warsaw (209), Wrocław (73) and Kraków (46).

Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg has announced plans to build a new factory in Poland producing counter-drone systems. The firm will invest over 200 million zloty (€46 million) in the facility, creating more than 100 long-term jobs.

“The new facility will support Polish industry and defence capabilities and strengthen Kongsberg’s presence in Poland,” declared CEO Eirik Lie alongside Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz at the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year serving as the official partner nation.

In January, Kongsberg signed an agreement to supply a new anti-drone system to Poland in partnership with Polish state defence group PGZ. The project comes in response to growing fears over the threat of Russian drones, around 20 of which violated Polish airspace on one night in September last year.

Norwegowie inwestują w Polsce. Duża inwestycja #Kongsberg na Pomorzu ogłoszona właśnie na #WSF2026. Szybka budowa fabryki i nowe miejsca pracy. pic.twitter.com/msI2FWGym8

Kosiniak-Kamysz thanked Kongsberg for its investment and emphasised that Polish-Norwegian relations are at their highest point in history, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

The announcement of the counter-drone plant came as Poland and Norway’s prime ministers, Donald Tusk and Jonas Gahr Støre, signed a declaration on strategic partnership that pledged to deepen security ties, including joint defence production and strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks.

While the exact location of the plant has not been revealed, Kongsberg stated that it would be in northern Poland, near the Tricity area (consisting of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot) on the Baltic Sea coast.

Construction of the facility is scheduled to begin this year, with production at the site scheduled to commence in the first half of 2028.

 

Counter-drone technology has become an increasing priority for Poland following Russian airspace violations and also the growing use by Moscow of jet-powered drones to strike targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border, including recently a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw.

Polish spending on drones and counter-drone systems combined rose from 100 million zloty in 2023 to 26 billion zloty in 2026, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk announced in August, quoted by news website Interia.

The summary report of this week’s Warsaw Security Forum suggested the use of counter-drone systems to create a “controlled fly-zone” over the Suwałki Gap, a strategically important choke point along the Polish-Lithuanian border that sits between the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and Russia’s ally Belarus.

Poland has signed an agreement for a new anti-drone system that it claims will be the first of its kind in Europe.

The network is intended to protect Poland’s eastern borders, where last year around 20 Russian drones crossed in an unprecedented incursion https://t.co/WhWhJxDwXA

Poland has in recent years moved to strengthen its defence ties with countries around the Baltic Sea. In January, it was announced that Poland will manufacture missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is purchasing from South Korea. Norway has already bought Piorun air-defence systems from Poland.

In 2024, Poland and Sweden signed a strategic partnership. The two countries subsequently held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic, and Poland this year ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab.

Saab this year also signed a strategic collaboration agreement with PGZ that will see them cooperate on naval production, servicing and technology.

On Monday this week, Norway’s defence ministry announced that Poland will join an initiative recently launched by 11 European countries and Canada to cooperate more closely on security in the North Atlantic, Arctic and Baltic Sea.

Wealthy Brits are accelerating plans to gift money to family members as fears over possible tax changes in the looming Autumn Budget grow.

Over 40 per cent of wealthy investors with an average wealth of £3.1m, said they have already gifted money or are seriously considering doing so over Budget worries, according to fresh analysis from Wealth Club.

Fears were centred on hiked taxes on savings and investments, with 63 per cent admitting they were concerned about increased tax bills. 

“They are clearly very concerned that this month’s Budget will mean bigger tax bills for them and are reacting accordingly,” said Alex Davies, founder and chief executive of Wealth Club.

“Whether it is gifting more money to children and families than they had planned or seeking out tax efficient investments it is important to remember that decisions in the Budget to tweak tax rules have real world consequences.”

Capital gains and Inheritance tax

In particular, wealthy investors expressed concerns over potential hikes to capital gains tax or inheritance tax (IHT).

Healey has reportedly rejected calls from senior Labour figures to raise capital gains tax to the same levels as income tax, after warnings it could harm the UK’s investment appeal.

But the Chancellor is said to be plotting a tax raid on family businesses in a bid to avoid spending cuts.  

The Chancellor is considering proposals to levy income tax when business owners hand their company down to their children, potentially almost doubling the tax bill, according to a report in the Telegraph.

Under current rules transfers can be structured in a way that allows them to attract capital gains tax which is charged at a lower rate.

Investors are already grappling with major changes to IHT introduced under former chancellor Rachel Reeves, including bringing pensions into the tax scopes, abolishing the non-dom regime and placing a 20 per cent levy on agricultural and business assets worth over £1m.

Speculation is also rising that Healey is considering introducing a lifetime gifting cap or adjusting the seven year exemption rule.

Dodging tax changes

Wealthy investors are also debating other courses of action in the lead up to the Budget to avoid a possible tax shakeup, including taking money from pension funds.

Nearly 30 per cent said they would put money into tax efficient vehicles, such as ISAs, while others are opting to delay investing until after the Budget.

Meanwhile, just over a quarter have sold investments and other assets, such as property, or retreated to the safety of cash.

Davies warned that if Healey opted to hike revenue, wealthy Brits would continue to look to avoid a large tax bill, leading them to “cut investment which is needed to support growing businesses” and the economy.

Sir James Dyson has called for “a new wave of technical universities” to be opened in the UK in order to boost young people’s skills. 

Dyson has endorsed a report by Policy Exchange demanding the opening of new engineering and construction qualifications in order to reduce the number of young people not in employment, education and training, known as ‘Neets’. 

The report by the right-leaning think tank said several towns and cities lacked a university of their own, which could be ripe for the opening of new academic centres providing skills to young people. 

The report aims to increase the number of graduates who have studied engineering or related subjects, with the proportion currently standing at less than 10 per cent. It argued that a new institution in Hereford, the New Model Institute for Technology and Engineering (NMITE) which opened in 2021, could lay the foundations for more universities to be built at a low cost. 

Dyson said: “Britain doesn’t produce enough engineers.

“Without them, we can’t make things, invent new products and technologies – or compete against the rest of the world. Britain needs many more places like these. This report shows how to build them.”

Dyson’s new intervention

Lord David Blunkett, the Blair-era education secretary, also backed research calling for “employer-focused” education, saying that upskilling young people would be essential for small businesses and large infrastructure projects over the next 10 years.

“[The report] argues convincingly that a new wave of NMITE-type institutions could contribute to the government’s goal of ensuring we ‘value the hard hat as much as the graduation cap’, providing valuable opportunities to talented young people in cold-spot communities, for whom the system is not delivering.”

Dyson has previously weighed in on the youth unemployment crisis, with official data showing that there are nearly 1m Neets. 

The inventor and billionaire has been a staunch critic of the Labour government, hitting out at the farming tax and saying the party had engaged in “revenge economics” by targeting wealthy people. 

In a column for The Sun in June last year, Dyson said entrepreneurs were choosing not to set up businesses in the UK .  

His latest intervention on technical education marks his ambition to influence the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, on public policy. 

The report said that the strongest cases for new technical universities came in areas such as Hartlepool, Barnsley and Grimsby. 

Authors at Policy Exchange propose a shorter and cheaper degree that involved students taking on less debt while employers such as Microsoft and BAE Systems could take more active roles in education, as at NMITE.

European bond and equity markets were hit by a fresh sell-off on Monday as the French government rolled out curfews to contain explosive riots that have spread across the country.

The 10-year yield on French bonds – a direct reflection of the government’s cost to borrow – spiked around 13 basis points to 4.9 per cent. The spread between French and German 10-year yields widened to its highest closing level since early 2012 as investors priced in the risk of ongoing unrest across the country.

The sell-off spread across the continent, with the 10-year yield in Italy – which is facing its own violent clashes – jumping 10 basis points.

“France appears to be heading for a fiscal crisis which could lead to contagion and potentially a recession in the euro-zone,” Andrew Kenningham, chief European economist at Capital Economics, said.

He added the crisis “brought the risk of fragmentation in the Euro-zone back to the fore”.

“A bigger crisis in France would lead to higher borrowing costs and lower growth in other Euro-zone economies. That said, contagion risks are a lot lower than they were in the 2010s,” Kenningham said.

French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu confirmed on Monday he has instructed prefectures, regional government representatives in France, to put in place “partial curfews” as he branded the “ultra-left” responsible for the unrest.

The French government has been plunged into crisis after demonstrations over the price of fuel and the condition of schools erupted into riots and looting.

Bad day for European equities

Volatility spilled over into equity markets and plunged the continents’ biggest indices into the red. France’s Cac 40 was down 1.5 per cent, Germany’s DAX 1.5 per cent and Amsterdam’s AEX 0.5 per cent.

Back in London, the FTSE 100 slumped 1.2 per cent led by a sell-off in miners and banks. The UK’s 10-year gilt yield inched up over four basis points, but analysts said bond markets were spared the worst impacts of the unrest in mainland Europe.

“While French bonds have come under renewed pressure as investors digest the latest political unrest, the picture in the UK has been considerably calmer, with gilts holding up relatively well ahead of next week’s Budget,” Richard Carter, head of fixed interest research, said. 

“That does not mean investors are short of things to worry about.”

He pointed to elevated tensions in the oil market as the conflict in the Middle East shows little sign of de-escalation. Brent crude traded above $108 on Monday afternoon, after a five per cent rally last week that sent prices to a five-month high.

Iran has upped its attacks on tankers in the region over the last week, with at least two container vessels disabled by mines.

John Healey’s potential tax raid on family businesses could make handing down companies to the next generation a “disaster” and damage the economy, advisers have warned.

The Chancellor is reportedly considering proposals to levy income tax when business owners hand down to their children, potentially almost doubling the bill.

Under current rules, transfers can be structured in a way that allows them to attract capital gains tax (CGT) which is charged at a lower rate, but Healey is debating a shake-up in a bid to increase revenue in his maiden Autumn Budget.

Tim Stovold, head of tax at Moore Kingston Smith, said: “If the proposals in the consultation are implemented as law, a number of transactions used to return value as a capital gain to a retiring generation, allowing their children to take over the ownership and running of the business, will become much more difficult or impossible.”

Investment appeal

Healey is debating shutting off a possible route owners frequently use to dodge a substantial one-off tax bill. Instead of selling the family business, partners convert holdings to ‘redeemable shares’, which the business can buy back using its own profits.

EU law protects market competition but has been used too little to help football fans. Worse still, Europe has helped the big clubs to increase their market power, writes Tsjalle van der Burg.

Football tickets have become expensive. Paris Saint-Germain currently top the European ranking: in 2024-25, the average admission price for a seat was €139. Barcelona, Real Madrid and four English clubs followed, while Bayern Munich was eighth at €79. Signs suggest ticket prices have risen further this year and the EU shares part of the blame for this.    

Fans like to watch a club that can win major trophies. In the past, there was much choice. In the 1970s, five clubs in France were national champions. In the past 10 years, by contrast, PSG have won eight times. So, anyone now wishing to see a French winner has fewer options, which implies competition in the French consumer market has decreased. This helps explain the high prices of tickets. Similar stories hold elsewhere.

In principle, EU competition law protects market competition. Unfortunately, it has been used too little to help football fans. Worse still, Europe has helped the big clubs to increase their market power.  

Bosman ruling 

This began in 1995 with the European Court of Justice’s Bosman ruling, which allowed players with expiring contracts to move clubs without a transfer fee. This benefited wealthy clubs and reduced competitive balance on the fields. The court’s motivation was that there should be free movement of workers. European rules are clear on this, and lawyers refer to this as “hard law”. 

During the case, football federations countered that the transfer system helped maintain competitive balance, making football more attractive and thus serving a public interest that should justify an exception to hard law. In Bosman, the judges found the competitive-balance argument relevant in principle, but after much consideration, hard law won.

However, the court overlooked a crucial point. Because less competitive balance means fewer clubs win major trophies, it also means less competition in consumer markets. That competition falls under hard law. By undermining market competition, the Bosman ruling itself contravened hard law.

The court should therefore have balanced the hard law of free movement of workers against the hard law of competition in consumer markets plus the soft law of the public interest of exciting matches. The outcome could have been different. In 2024, the court’s Diarra ruling further weakened the transfer system, with a motivation similar to that in Bosman.

Royal Antwerp ruling

The European Court of Justice’s 2023 Royal Antwerp ruling could further undermine competitive balance. Royal Antwerp concerns Uefa’s rules mandating clubs to have a quota of “homegrown” players. A Belgian court could judge it this week and is expected to weaken or end the rule. 

One of the rule’s objectives is to improve competitive balance by limiting rich clubs from fielding only the world’s top players. Research suggests it achieves this effect, though more study is needed. Unfortunately, this effect was sidelined in Royal Antwerp. This was incorrect. 

To the extent that the rule promotes competitive balance, it also promotes competition in consumer markets. This provides a hard-law argument for the rule, which the court should have examined thoroughly. I hope the Belgian court will ask the European Court to explain why it did not. Does justice really mean that judges can ignore the benefits of low prices for fans? 

European Super League

Another reason for declining competitiveness is the attempted European Super League which, although aborted, led investors to seek a court order to prevent Uefa from imposing sanctions on similar future projects. The European Court largely agreed, arguing that competition organisers should be free to compete.

This decision once again ignored consumer markets. Any form of Super League would mean fewer clubs could win the European title, thereby reducing competition in consumer markets. 

EU competition law prohibits agreements between clubs (and concerted practices) that restrict market competition. Every Super League, and any threat thereof, violates these rules because it is based on an agreement between clubs (or a concerted practice) that restricts competition in consumer markets. The European competition authorities should therefore have banned all Super Leagues and associated threats long ago.

Without the threat of a Super League, Europe’s major clubs would have had less power. Democratic decision-making within the football federations, where small clubs and small countries hold most of the votes, would have regained prominence, leading to more competitive balance, more market competition, and lower prices.

EU sports legislation  

Such an outcome is still possible. Supporters’ organisations could go to court and demand that competition law be enforced. But it might be even better if they joined the call for special EU sports legislation, demanding that it should promote competitive balance and competition in consumer markets, making the game less expensive and more exciting.

Unfortunately, the EU has done little to help fans so far. This raises a question: is the EU willing to uphold competition law to benefit fans, small clubs and overall welfare even if it comes at a cost to large clubs and wealthy investors? Or is Europe a project that mainly honours the lawyers and lobbyists of the rich?

Tsjalle van der Burg is an assistant professor of economics and now a researcher at the University of Twente in the Netherlands. This article is based on a longer article on LSE Blogs.

The full-size Range Rover Electric has the ultra-luxury EV market largely to itself. The cheaper, sportier Range Rover Sport Electric faces a far bigger fight, and JLR needs it to win.

It has been quite a week for JLR. Jaguar finally revealed its £130,000 Type 01 in New York on Tuesday, but the car that matters far more to the group’s balance sheet went on sale a few days earlier. Range Rover has been JLR’s profit engine for years, cushioning everything from Jaguar’s sales collapse to this summer’s job cuts. In the three months to June, Range Rover, Range Rover Sport and Defender made up more than 80% of the cars JLR shipped, so the new Range Rover Sport Electric has to prove that the group’s most important brand can keep the money coming without an engine.

That’s a tougher job than it sounds, because the two electric Range Rovers share a great deal of engineering but sit in very different parts of the market. The full-size Range Rover Electric costs upwards of £150,000 and has very few obvious rivals, while the Sport Electric starts at £109,810 and lands in a far more crowded corner, where Porsche, BMW and Mercedes all have big electric SUVs chasing the same buyers.

Range Rover Sport Electric price and specs

The Sport Electric opens with the Dynamic SE at £109,810, with the Autobiography at £122,780 and the launch First Edition at £126,290, and orders are open now.

The core ingredients come straight from the bigger car. A motor on each axle produces a combined 550bhp, powered by a 118.5kWh usable battery on an 800-volt system, and Land Rover claims a 10 to 80 per cent charge in 22 minutes on a suitable 350kW charger. Official range is 374 miles, two more than the full-size Range Rover Electric, although Land Rover itself quotes around 333 miles for real-world driving. That’s a refreshingly frank figure from a car maker, and probably the one to plan around.

How is the Range Rover Sport Electric different?

Land Rover has given the Sport its own chassis set-up to make it feel more agile than its bigger sibling. The full-size Range Rover Electric drops its active anti-roll system, because the heavy battery lowers the centre of gravity enough that the body leans less on its own, and losing the hardware saves weight, cost and energy. The Sport keeps it, alongside air suspension with twin-valve dampers, four-wheel steering and software that shuffles power between the axles.

Land Rover says the structure is 61% stiffer than previous Sport models, with a centre of gravity 73mm lower than the petrol and diesel versions. With 550bhp and well over two tonnes to manage, all that hardware has plenty of work to do.

What is the Range Rover Sport Electric like to drive?

We haven’t driven it yet, and the press won’t get behind the wheel of production cars until later in the year. A handful of outlets have tried prototypes, though, and the early signs are good. Evo found the four-wheel steering gave the Sport the agility a car this size needs, turning tightly at low speed while staying composed, and said the instant torque made tricky off-road obstacles smoother and less fraught than in the combustion versions. PistonHeads came away describing a car that felt quicker to turn and lighter on its feet than you’d expect, and impressively capable off the tarmac.

Those were short drives in prototypes, so we’d call them encouraging and leave it there until we’ve driven one ourselves. They do suggest Land Rover has managed the trick it needed to, making a heavy electric SUV feel smaller than it is.

If you’re thinking of selling your car, or just want to know what it’s worth, get a free car valuation with Regit in a couple of minutes.

Range Rover Sport Electric vs Porsche Cayenne Electric

The Porsche Cayenne S Electric is where the Sport’s job gets hardest. It starts at £99,900, around £10,000 less than the Range Rover, it claims more range at up to 405 miles, and as PistonHeads pointed out, it’s half a second quicker to 62mph. Porsche also has the stronger reputation among performance-minded buyers, and the base Cayenne Electric undercuts the Range Rover by even more.

Land Rover’s answer is the Range Rover name, which Porsche can’t copy, and everything that comes with it, including proper off-road ability. Electric motors suit rough terrain because they deliver their torque instantly and can be controlled very precisely, and the Sport Electric keeps the hardware and software that set a Range Rover apart. Most of these cars will spend their lives outside schools, offices and restaurants, a long way from any muddy hillside, but knowing your car could cope is a big part of why people buy into the Range Rover idea in the first place.

Why going electric is a big test for Range Rover

Chris Ashton-Green, founder and chief executive of motoring platform Regit, thinks a lot is riding on this, but he’s backing Range Rover to pull it off. “Range Rover is arguably the most iconic British car still being made, and it’s one of the real shining lights of British motoring,” he says. “Going electric won’t be easy, but I think it has every chance. People buy a Range Rover for the name, the history and what it says about them, and JLR has spent decades building that up. Swapping the engine for a battery doesn’t take any of that away, and if anything, the quietness adds to the overall feel of luxury. I think people will really buy into it.”

The challenge is real, though, because other premium brands have found the switch painful. The Porsche Taycan has become the cautionary tale, with US pricing data suggesting it can lose around 55 to 60 per cent of its value in five years. When you’re spending six figures on a car, what it’s worth when you sell it matters almost as much as how it drives, and steep depreciation has put plenty of luxury buyers off going electric.

The good news is that the market looks to be turning. Motorway’s latest National Car Index found that used EV sales on its platform more than doubled this summer compared with the same period last year, with the average price sellers received up 6%. If used electric car values keep firming up, one of the biggest reasons to hesitate over a £110,000 EV starts to fade, and that could be very good timing for the Sport Electric.

Range Rover Sport Electric pros and cons

What’s good – Range Rover luxury and badge appeal in a more agile package – Fast 800V charging, with 10 to 80 per cent in a claimed 22 minutes – Keeps the off-road ability rivals can’t match – Land Rover quotes a realistic real-world range alongside the official figure

What’s not – Around £10,000 more than a Porsche Cayenne S Electric – The Porsche goes further on a charge and is quicker to 62mph – No production-car drives yet, only short prototype tests – Luxury EVs have a history of heavy depreciation

Range Rover Sport Electric verdict

The full-size Range Rover Electric can charge a premium simply for being the biggest, most imposing electric Range Rover you can buy, while the Sport Electric has to justify costing more than a quicker, longer-range Porsche. That makes its job harder.

We think it will manage it all the same. Range Rover luxury, real off-road ability and a chassis built to make 550bhp feel manageable is a combination nobody else offers at this price, and plenty of buyers will happily pay £10,000 more for the badge alone. For JLR, at the end of a week when it bet Jaguar’s future on a brand-new car, the Sport Electric is a timely reminder of where the money really comes from, and it looks well placed to keep it coming.

Global demand for Scotch appears to be holding up reasonably well, but there is clearly no shortage of supply. With bulging warehouses, distillers have cut production, causing real grief to the farmers and maltsters who supply them. Ron Emler investigates …    

This year’s British summer, the hottest on record, left a scorched trail down the East Coast barley belt that feeds the whisky industry. After two months without significant rain, East Anglia’s fields began to resemble the Sahara. 

Conditions eased moving north, with Scotland experiencing its sixth warmest summer on record, yet yields were down, particularly of spring barley, which provides around four-fifths of malting-quality grain. The Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB) reported yields were 17 per cent below the five-year mean.

Anthony Hopkins, AHDB director, cereals and oilseeds, said: “This is the second, or in some cases third, successive challenging harvest. At a time of high input costs, arable farmers in the worst-affected areas are really feeling the financial pressure.”  

According to Farmers Weekly, the historic price gap between malting and feed barley has shrunk to just £5 -15 per tonne. In certain areas, malting barley prices have periodically dropped below feed barley, which makes growing it unviable for many farmers given the stricter quality specs demanded.

Those low returns have driven farmers to reduce plantings. According to AHDB for this year’s harvest 930,000 hectares were under barley, 12 per cent less than in 2025 and marking a 16-year low. In Scotland, the area fell by 13 per cent to 258,000 ha. the lowest since 1960.

Last year Scottish farmers harvested a bumper crop of more than 2m tonnes, though there were many rejections due to high levels of nitrogen or poor screening levels that failed to meet the stringent specs imposed on malted barley by the distillers.

Right now, those supplying this key raw ingredient are really feeling the pinch. “We are in a major downturn,” says Colin Johnston, Sales and Marketing Director of Crisp Malt. “Whisky production is substantially down and there is a drop of about 300,000 tons in demand for malt.”

This has put strain on maltsters, with one in Pencaitland, East Lothian, closing earlier this year and others sitting on investment plans until the market for Scotch whisky begins to rise again.

As the production slowdown accelerated into 2025 and 2026, the maltsters found themselves over-contracted. By buying more grain than was needed, they ended up with excess stocks. Ironically, this year’s short harvest has come as a relief.

“There is a ‘weather” market, but there is also a ‘geopolitical’ market,” says Johnston. While the blocking of the Straits of Hormuz has had no effect on cereal supplies in Europe, malting grain prices rose in August and September because the war between Russia and Ukraine effectively closed shipping through the Black Sea. 

Financial pressure

There are some glimmers of hope that the distillers might soon begin to gently increase output as global demand for Scotch whisky picks up.

Data from the UK’s Food and Drink Federation showed a 5.8 per cent increase in volume in UK whisky exports in the first six months of 2026, while value rose by 2.2 per cent to £2.5bn.

Nevertheless, distillers still feel they need to drain the surplus from their warehouses before demand for malting barley can return to more normal levels.

“The industry is sitting on a lot of stock and it’s going to take quite some time to work through that”, says Colin Johnston. “The market will be suppressed for a while. When that changes is crystal-ball stuff. Nobody really knows.”

This all begs the question of whether UK barley farmers will continue to plant the crop or if the land devoted to it will continue to shrink.

The perceived wisdom is that growers South of the Border have more options as the warming climate favours less traditional crops and there is wider access to environmental schemes. Scottish growers may have fewer options than to accept the on-going low prices.

One scenario supposes that demand for Scotch whisky improves rapidly, not least because of the UK-India trade pact, which could reverse the equation and push up barley prices at just the time farmers are turning their backs on the crop,

“We have to find a way to keep barley farming attractive for them,” says Johnston, noting that the loss of EU subsidies was a heavy blow, and that European grain is less expensive to produce because of lower energy costs.

“The drive now from distillers is for the agricultural sector to try to decarbonise and try to become more efficient in the use of fertilisers – which are fossil fuel-based,” he says.

“So, there’re lots of initiatives around regenerative agriculture, using cover cropping as alternative green fertilisers, monitoring nitrogen use efficiency, plus using technology to ensure that fertilisers are only being applied where the crop requires it.”

Where they can, maltsters are working with farmers to encourage sustainable techniques which are appropriate to their specific land and region. 

Sustainable farming

That is part of a pattern of research and change around the globe. Canadian farmers are backing experimentation into more prolific and resilient barley varieties such as Churchill while the giant US brewer and distiller Constellation Brands is investing an additional $100m over the next five years to support farmers in Idaho, Montana and North Dakota. The aim is to strengthen its supply chain and back initiatives to improve the resilience and long-term sustainability of their farming operations. 

Facing low returns, will UK barley farmers be willing to absorb the costs of changing growing patterns and new varieties to meet the increasing demands from distillers eager to burnish their environmental credentials? 

“The cost of this transition has to be shared across the supply chain and can’t reasonably be expected to land squarely on the farmers shoulders”, says Colin Johnston.

John Healey has reportedly drawn up plans for a tax raid on family businesses ahead of his first Budget, as he scrambles to avoid spending cuts.

The Chancellor is considering proposals to levy income tax when business owners hand their company down to their children, potentially almost doubling the tax bill, according to a report in the Telegraph.

Under current rules transfers can be structured in a way that allows them to attract capital gains tax which is charged at a lower rate.

The plans would hit entrepreneurs preparing to retire, with accountants warning Healey’s plot could drive many family businesses into “extinction” and discourage new companies opening their doors.

The Treasury is looking to raise hundreds of millions on top of Rachel Reeves’ raid on family businesses through inheritance tax (IHT). The previous Chancellor’s crackdown is expected to generate £300m a year.

Turning off the tap

Healey is mulling whether to shut off a possible route of handing down a business that owners frequently use upon retirement to prevent a substantial one-off tax bill.

Instead of selling the family firm to the next generation, partners convert holdings into ‘redeemable shares’ which the business can buy back using its own profits.

This move attracts capital gains tax (CGT) which is charged at 24 per cent for higher-rate taxpayers, compared to 45 per cent on income tax.

Cutting off the CGT route of handing down a company could lead to a swelling tax bill, while selling on the open market still leaves the business exposed to being taxed as a capital gain.

Business owners are already feeling the effects of a wave of red tape introduced under the workers’ rights changes introduced by Angela Rayner alongside minimum wage increases and soaring energy bills caused by the conflict in the Middle East.

The global tech giant, which had previously planned to fund a supercomputer at the site, has ended its involvement in the partnership following concerns over supply issues.

It is planning to list on the New York Stock Exchange – with a target valuation of reportedly up to $35bn – while maintaining its British domicile.

The London-based firm, which has former deputy prime minister Nick Clegg and former Meta executive Sheryl Sandberg as members of its board, reported a net of loss of $1bn on revenues of $141m in the first half of the year, with the bulk of losses caused by non-cash charges.

    Facing allegations of racism, bigotry and sexism, can Nigel Farage clean up Reform UK’s act? It’s not even clear that he wants to, writes Eliot Wilson

    The news that a year-long undercover investigation by ITV News has revealed racism, bigotry and sexism among a number of Reform UK’s candidates and office-holders was not a surprise. This problem has deep roots.

    Former currency trader and hotelier Catherine Blaiklock established the Brexit Party, out of which Reform UK grew, with Nigel Farage’s support in January 2019. She lasted exactly two months as its leader before Farage took over, after she was revealed to have written and retweeted racist social media posts. Her own work included “Islam = submission – mostly to raping men it seems” and “I want my country back. I want seaside donkeys on the beach and little village churches, not acid attacks, mobs and mosques”. She also retweeted 45 posts by Mark Collett of the BNP including a caption of a photograph of a classroom of multiracial pupils which read “This is a British school. This is white genocide.”

    During the last general election campaign, the party had to disassociate itself from three parliamentary candidates. One accused immigrants from sub-Saharan Africa of “diluting” the UK’s collective IQ and another said black people should “get off [their] lazy arses” and stop acting “like savages”. A third responded to news of a boat carrying illegal migrants landing at Dover by saying, “I hope I’m near one of the scumbags one day I won’t run away I’ll slaughter them then have their family taken out”.

    At the time, Farage defended his party by claiming it had been “so desperate for people to stand that people stood, and then we employed a big vetting company who didn’t do the job”. He also argued that Reform UK had “an awful lot of candidates being stitched up in the most extraordinary way, with quotes taken out of context”.

    Reform faces fresh revelations

    Last week’s documentary, ITV Exposure—Undercover: A Year in Reform, was more comprehensive but wholly recognisable. Alan Feeley, a Reform UK councillor in Solihull, described Asian people as “absolute parasites” and wanted the authorities to “drag them out of their homes, stick them on planes and f*** them off to Pakistan”. He expressed the belief that “no more than one per cent of British population can be non-white”.

    Dean Miller, a councillor in Bromley, played fast and loose with the Treason Act 1351 when he said: “Apparently, King Charles is a fucking Muslim.. cut the cunt’s head off”. He claimed that immigrants had “come to rape and pillage and fucking kill us”, and that white people had “been ethnically cleansed out of London”. He added, “Like all the ethnic fucking kids, they’re not white, they’re all fucking black, and they’re like fucking animals. It’s horrible to say it. I’m not racist.”

    The response of Reform UK and its leader to these accusations has been predictable and rote. A statement said that “from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting. This is the same for all organisations”. However, the party claims to have “improved and prioritised its vetting procedures”, a promise Farage made more than two years ago. It has seemingly not been especially successful.

    Attack is the best form of defence. Reform UK also criticised ITV’s “extreme methods of deception”. Richard Tice, the party’s deputy leader, alleged that one figure was “a Tory plant” who was “deliberately saying some things to make us look bad”. Reform UK may not need much assistance in that area. There were also accusations of entrapment, although it is not clear how people who are not racist are so easily “entrapped” into making such enthusiastically racist remarks.

    Robert Jenrick, the former pro-Remain, centrist Conservative MP who managed to be dropped from Cabinet for lapses of propriety by Boris Johnson, dismissed the most recent allegations against Reform UK as “bad apples”. He misunderstands the proverb. It does not show that every sample has a few sub-standard elements; rather it warns that one malign presence can be corrosive to a whole group, or, as was more pithily written in 1340, “a rotten apple quickly infects its neighbour”.

    Can Reform UK ever be a serious party?

    Reform UK, despite seeming to be running out of momentum in opinion polls, attempts to present itself as a serious potential party of government. It cannot do so with any credibility while racists are dismissed as bad apples, vague promises are made of improved vetting procedures, accusations of serious financial impropriety are brushed aside by a smirking Farage and the party’s fundamental and universal defence is “a big boy did it and ran away”.

    Nigel Farage is probably the most influential British politician of the 21st century so far, and he has proven himself often a brilliant campaigner. But he is not a leader of a party. He has carved out a 30-year career as the carney barker for a shifting coalition of the aggrieved: anti-EU, anti-immigration, anti-woke, anti-lockdown, anti-net zero. You cannot build a political party on the platform of “Fings Ain’t Wot They Used T’Be”.

    There will be a general election in less than three years; less than three months, if some rumours are to be believed. The window is closing for Farage to demonstrate that he can turn Reform UK into a political party in a meaningful sense, and that he wants to. The jury is out on both counts.

    Eliot Wilson is a writer and historian. He is a senior fellow for national security at the Coalition for Global Prosperity and a contributing editor at Defence on the Brink

    Firms may be reluctant to admit when AI goes wrong, but industries like aviation show why sharing those near misses matters, writes Freya Russell

    Embarrassment originates from the French embarrasser, which more literally translates as “to block”. When it comes to safer AI, embarrassment does just that: it blocks a golden opportunity to share for the greater good. 

    When AI makes a mistake, no matter how small or large, if it is caught before it reaches a client, the natural inclination is to sweep the near miss under the carpet. There has been no harm to the firm, and admitting a mistake can invite consequences that extend far beyond the original error. So, why would a firm admit to such a narrow escape? The premise is that they would if the repercussions of a confession were to be removed.

    AI is already embedded in financial services; HM Treasury reports that 75 per cent of financial services firms are already using AI in at least one business function. With each implementation comes new lessons: areas where AI performs poorly, where human judgement was needed and what controls prevented a mistake. The number of these experiences is considerable, yet we are failing to do anything with them. Collectively, these present an opportunity for industry-wide progress. 

    Aviation: A model for reporting mistakes

    Financial services has an opportunity to follow a precedent set by the aviation sector decades ago. Celebrating its 50th anniversary this year, NASA’s Aviation Safety Reporting System has collected more than 2.3m voluntary, confidential reports, which are analysed and shared with the wider aviation community. One airline’s experience can help another avoid making the same mistake. HM Treasury is now proposing that financial services apply this principle to AI through a confidential, voluntary repository for reporting AI incidents and near misses.

    Making the repository confidential is a step in the right direction; having the incidents and remedies limited to a select group reduces the risk of fallout. However, the issue of embarrassment remains. Research in the Journal of Business Ethics on risk reporting in financial services found that “fear, embarrassment, guilt… should not be understated”. This shame is not merely an individual emotion; it can become an organisational incentive to keep quiet. For the repository to be a success, a more ambitious approach is needed. Chatham House Rules would reduce the reputational risk of speaking openly; if this measure were in place any addition to the repository could not be traceable to a particular firm. With the embarrassment factor eliminated, the next hurdle the proposal faces is perhaps more fundamental. 

    Where does competitive advantage end, and where does collective resilience begin? Refining governance structures and understanding the practicalities of deploying AI systems takes considerable time and resources, and sharing these hard-won lessons may feel like self-sabotage. Conventional wisdom holds that such innovation should be protected as a source of competitive edge, rather than shared with others. The repository will only achieve its aims if firms believe that some knowledge creates greater value when shared than when protected.

    Sharing AI expertise is not a zero-sum game

    At this point it is critical to be clear about the distinction between technological innovation and governance. Better AI models create a competitive advantage; better AI governance should not. Whilst keeping near misses within the firm may be a benefit in the short term, in the long run it leaves the wider sector weaker. Responsible AI usage is not a zero-sum game; when one organisation discovers an effective safeguard, sharing it would provide a benefit to others at no cost to the originating firm.

    In many ways, the proposal represents a departure from how financial services has traditionally learned from risk. The governance frameworks that define the industry today were often imposed or accelerated in response to collapses and bubbles, rather than in anticipation of them. The Financial Services AI Adoption Plan takes a refreshingly proactive approach. Instead of waiting for a monumental AI catastrophe to force the industry’s hand, it captures early warnings before they culminate in a crisis.

    The need for such a framework is reinforced by the pace at which AI is developing. Lord Clement-Jones, who is recognised as a leading parliamentary authority on AI, warns that the pace of technological advancement could “outrun our capacity to govern it”. Governance therefore needs to evolve at a faster pace, and for that to happen a major change needs to occur. The repository is just the type of change that is needed, it would allow firms to adapt to emerging evidence provided by their peers.

    The industry must learn to treat a near miss as an opportunity to improve, rather than an embarrassment to conceal. Ultimately, the biggest obstacle to safer AI is less technological and more cultural; the challenge is creating conditions in which firms are willing to share what they have learnt from implementing AI systems, without the risk of repercussions. If this is done, the industry can start learning before failure, rather than because of it.

    Freya Russell is AI committee chair at a fintech, where she works on AI implementation and governance

    As the UK prepares to host the G20 presidency in 2027, it has an opportunity to bring international partners together and help shape the global conversation on trusted AI, writes Susan Langley

    The UK’s reputation as a global financial centre rests on more than the strength of its markets, the depth of its talent or the reach of its international networks. It also rests on trust. 

    I’ve often said this year that capital goes where it feels welcome and stays where it’s secure. Investors need confidence that the rules are clear, that risks are managed and that the institutions underpinning our financial system uphold the highest standards. Our regulators, respected around the world, are central to providing that confidence, helping make the UK a place where businesses want to invest and grow. 

    This week, I will host the Financial Conduct Authority and the Prudential Regulation Authority at the City Regulators’ Dinner. I will make clear that maintaining high standards must go hand in hand with a regulatory framework that keeps pace with advances in artificial intelligence (AI), digital assets and tokenisation. 

    The financial centres that thrive are those that combine robust regulation with an environment that enables innovation. Striking that balance will be essential to ensuring the UK remains competitive as the global financial landscape evolves. 

    The City of London Corporation’s Regulating for Growth report, published last year, set out practical recommendations for more predictable and proportionate regulation, reducing unnecessary burdens and strengthening engagement between regulators and industry. It’s not a call for wall-to-wall deregulation or the City becoming the wild west of financial hubs, it’s about greater flexibility and simplification in our financial hub. 

    We welcome the progress made since its publication, and the commitment from regulators to deliver a framework that supports growth while maintaining the standards on which the UK’s reputation depends.  

    London can lead the AI conversation

    Working across industry, government and regulators is exactly what the UK needs to do to enhance its regulatory framework. Initiatives such as OFI Financial Services, a single front door and concierge service for international firms looking to expand in the UK, is a prime example. By helping businesses navigate the regulatory landscape and understand requirements earlier, we can make it easier to invest here. 

    International investors consistently tell us that clarity and predictability of the long-term direction of regulation are important when deciding where to invest. The next challenge is to ensure that the progress we have made translates into a consistently positive experience for firms of all sizes. That becomes even more important as technology reshapes financial services. 

    AI has enormous potential to improve productivity and unlock new products and services. Digital assets and tokenisation could transform how financial instruments are traded creating opportunities to make markets more efficient and accessible. It really feels like with AI and emerging digital tech, we’re at the start of another Industrial Revolution and the financial services sector can be at the forefront of that in the UK. 

    The UK has made a promising start. Regulatory sandboxes, of which the UK was the first to introduce, and have since been replicated in 50 other jurisdictions, offer businesses opportunities to test new technologies in controlled environments, supporting experimentation while protecting consumers and financial stability. 

    Financial markets increasingly operate across borders, while emerging technologies can be deployed internationally at speed. Divergent regulatory approaches risk creating fragmentation, increasing costs for businesses and making it harder to manage risks consistently. 

    We therefore need greater international cooperation on the use of AI in financial services. Common principles, stronger regulatory interoperability and closer collaboration between standard-setting bodies can help firms innovate across markets while maintaining robust safeguards. 

    As the UK prepares to host the G20 presidency in 2027, it has an opportunity to bring international partners together and help shape the global conversation on trusted AI. 

    The Prime Minister has set out an ambition for the UK to help shape the international agenda on AI. Financial services should be an important part of that effort. By drawing on our expertise in financial regulation, we can help build approaches that encourage innovation while maintaining public confidence. 

    Now we must build on the UK’s record of world-leading regulation, working together at home and internationally to ensure that our regulatory strengths remain a source of competitive advantage.

    Susan Langley is the Lady Mayor of the City of London
